utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Could we have the accused brought in, please? (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Does everybody hear? Are the interpreters ready? Again, good morning. Does the Prosecution hear? The Defence? Mr. Blaskic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing, continuing the interviews of those people who have been called by the Prosecution. Go ahead, Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The Prosecutor would now like to call Lieutenant Colonel Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: About how long have you scheduled for your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Approximately two and a half hours, your Honour. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Do you hear me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing. Would you give us your name again, please? You are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Geoffrey Martyn Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Before testifying, please read the solemn declaration, which you are asked to read pursuant to the rules of procedure and evidence. LIEUTENANT COLONEL THOMAS (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Colonel, you were called in by the Prosecution as part of the charges that were brought by the Prosecutor against General Blaskic. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Colonel Thomas, you have given your name to the court. Could you please give your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: British.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regular army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year did you join the British army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you just -- briefly I would like you to give some background to the court, very briefly. Whereabouts did you do your officer training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Sandhurst.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the Royal Military Academy in Sandhurst and that is, I think, equivalent to West Point in the United States or Sancerre in France?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long was that period of training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 14 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the training centred around while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially it is leadership training, based on low-level infantry skills to develop leaders to, at that stage, command platoons or their equivalent in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you answer my questions, if you could address the judges rather than me? Thank you. Which part of the army did you join when you left Sandhurst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was commissioned in the Cheshire Regiment which is an infantry regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were commissioned as a second lieutenant into the army, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what year that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you joined your Regiment, the Cheshire Regiment, on a four-month emergency tour in Londonderry in Northern Ireland, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To give some background, because you are going to be talking about this in your particularly relevant testimony, what is the size of a British infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It varies on the particular role they are in at the time, whether they are based in Germany or the United Kingdom or in Northern Ireland, but usually between about 550 and 750 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that that battalion is then subdivided down into companies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many companies are there normally in a battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are normally three rifle companies or fighting companies, to give it a simple explanation, a support company and a headquarters company.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those companies are then divided down again into platoons, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, the Cheshire Regiment; why is it called the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, in common with a lot of British army regiments which have a long history, we were raised in 1689 in the county of Cheshire, in the north west of England, and we recruit nearly all our soldiers from that particular part of the country. As I say, in common with most of the British Army, the army has very strong regional connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think after your service in Northern Ireland, the Regiment, the Cheshire Regiment went to Germany, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was actually in Germany at the time, they went to Northern Ireland from Germany, but yes, I did return to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the role of the battalion in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were then what was called a mechanised battalion, we had armoured personnel carriers, and we were at that time involved in, if you like, along with much of NATO at that time, defending against the then perceived Soviet threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think your job then was as platoon commander, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many men did you command at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that was from 1978 to 1979, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then completed an in-service degree in politics at the University of Bristol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1979 to 1982. You then returned to the Regiment in 1982 and you were second in command of an infantry company in Ballykelly in Northern Ireland, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your job --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, think about the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. I will slow down. What is the role of a second in command in an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He stands in for the company commander when he is away, he does a lot of the routine administration of the company and basically helps to run the company with the company commander. It is the sort of job that a young Captain would normally do and at that particular time, the company commander was, of course -- was Major Stewart, who subsequently went on to command the battalion when I was one of his company commanders later in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were a Captain at this time and this was from 1982 to 1984?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1984 to 1985, the battalion moved to Hong Kong as part of the British military garrison, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Hong Kong I was the adjutant of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the role of the adjutant within an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are the commanding officer's principal staff officer, responsible for the day-to-day administration of the battalion for what we call G1 matters, administration, discipline, that sort of thing. As I say, really you are essentially the commanding officer's executive officer. You are also responsible, particularly in Hong Kong, for the ceremonial side of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Hong Kong has now gone back to China and the British military garrison has withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1985, I think you returned to the Royal Military Academy in Sandhurst, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities at this time, at the Military Academy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was what was called a company instructor, I had three platoons over the two-year period of officer cadets, each platoon being again about 30 cadets, and I was responsible for taking the cadets from day one of their training to when they were commissioned 7 months later and basically ran their training along with the other staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This was based around infantry training and tactics, primarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially low-level infantry tactics up to company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were essentially training the future leaders of the British army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think then from 1987 to 1988, you were again in a training position in a territorial infantry battalion based in the United Kingdom, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then I think in 1988 you were selected for Army Staff College, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that involved training for you at the Royal Military College of Science at Shrivenham and at the Staff College in Camberley, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did this training involve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of the course was ten months at Shrivenham, which is a science-based course to prepare army officers for staff jobs in the Ministry of Defence and other scientific establishments -- other establishments whereby they may be involved, for example in the procurement of weapon systems, in the staffing and purchase of weapon systems and that sort of thing, and it was essentially a science-based course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could slow down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we have the same concern here. I know all these questions are important, but he is telling us his life. He is available to you, you called him, I suppose he is going to say what he can about the conflict in which he was involved. Perhaps all these questions could be summarised quickly. We would be sensitive to that. If you say that it is particularly relevant, of course, continue in that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have a few more questions. My view is I call the -- the Prosecutor calls this witness and he is a military man and in order to provide some foundation for the basis of his testimony, I think it is relevant that you actually hear about his military career and what he will base some of his opinions on. As I say, I only have a few more questions, but I do think it is relevant and I do think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The training at Staff College, you say this is to prepare officers of the British army for staff jobs. I think it is also true, is it not, that Staff College is there to prepare, as it were, the future leaders of the British army, those persons who are destined for higher rank, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly provides a foundation to go on in the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were then promoted to Major in 1989, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then actually carried out what is known as a staff job with headquarters United Kingdom Land Forces in Wilton in Salisbury, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did that job involve, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially it was largely in the training world and I was involved in staffing matters of training policy for the army across a wide range, really, which I will not go into detail here about, but it was a training policy job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think in 1992 you then returned to command a company with the Cheshire Regiment, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many men are there in a company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time, and it is probably more relevant to what we are going on to, I was commanding a company of about 100 men in Germany and at this time we were what was called an armoured infantry battalion, so we were equipped with Warrior vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it was at this time that the Cheshire Regiment actually deployed to Bosnia passes as part of the United Nations Protection Force, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. We were warned in August 1992 that we were likely to be part of the first British deployment. We then prepared between August 1992 and November 1992 and we then deployed with all our armoured vehicles in early November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will come back to that, but I just want to bring the court up to date with your career. I think after your return from Bosnia, you went back to Germany, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where you continued to command a company and then in fact you moved on to another training job with the armoured infantry training team in Senelager in Germany, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there you trained British army personnel for service in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the UN Protection Force and subsequently with NATO forces, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was certainly part of the job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you actually instructed, am I right, on the tactical use of the Warrior armoured fighting vehicle, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could ask for the first exhibit to be placed in front of the witness, these exhibits have been premarked. This is exhibit number 100 and the image is Z1/169. Mr. President, we are using new technology this morning. The image appears on the screen. You will be talking a lot about the Warrior and I think just for a point of reference for the court, this is a Warrior armoured fighting vehicle, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the vehicle that was extensively used by the British infantry battalion in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when you refer to "Warrior" you are referring to this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think then from 1996 to 1997, you were chief of staff for training support command in Germany, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, just to bring us right up to date, in February of this year you were promoted to Lieutenant Colonel and given command of the third battalion, the Cheshire Regiment, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many men do you currently have under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Thomas, you are, are you not, a professional army officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you have been for 20 years, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How familiar would you say you are with infantry training and tactics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you will have heard from my testimony, I have been involved in a fair number of training jobs, so yes, I am very familiar with infantry tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the infantry training and tactics of other armies other than the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously to a much lesser degree, but as part of training, certainly at Sandhurst and Staff College, one did study the tactics of the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now we come on to your particularly relevant testimony. I wish you to recall the events that occurred between November 1992 and April 1993 when you were a company commander of a company, the Cheshire Regiment in Central Bosnia. I think you have already said, and if this is correct please confirm it, the Cheshire Regiment was part of the British government's contribution to the United Nations Protection Force, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you deployed to Bosnia with elements of British cavalry and also certain logistics or supply troops, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the modus operandi of the Cheshire Regiment in Bosnia? What was your mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were absolutely clear in the fact that our mission was to support the United Nations Commission for Refugees in the distribution of aid throughout Central Bosnia. That was essentially our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And to, as it were, provide protection for those actually attempting to supply humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th November 1992, although I had been on a reconnaissance in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at Split, we spent a couple of days offloading our Warriors from the ship. We then low-loaded to Tomislavgrad and then drove them over the mountains into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were located, were you not, in the town of Vitez in Central Bosnia, the battalion headquarters was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the majority of the soldiers in the battalion. How long did you actually spend in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there for very long initially, I spent about two or three weeks there, barely time to unpack, before I was despatched up to a small town called Kladanj, about 50 kilometres south of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could indicate on the map next to you the location of Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it is really in the north eastern corner of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Take a seat now. What was your function in Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular time we were very concerned about the situation in Tuzla, which was deteriorating rapidly, and there were also reports that some of the enclaves were in severe difficulties. At that time we began to hear about Srebrenica. It was felt we ought to have a presence in the north eastern part of Bosnia, so I was sent up there with a small team to establish a link in that area, and what we were then tasked to do was to escort convoys along a stretch of road from Kladanj into Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, if you could slow down and try and follow my pace. I know it feels unnatural, but the interpreters ... I think you commenced these duties in Kladanj and then at the end of December you moved your entire company to Tuzla, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you based in the town of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were based in an airfield, a former Yugoslavian airforce airfield about 8 kilometres to the south east of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it was very much as best we could to escort aid throughout the area of Tuzla and north of Tuzla to open up routes as best we could, to carry out liaison with the factions on the ground, to establish some sort of dialogue with the Serb forces who were to the north and east of Tuzla and also to meet, there was a regular convoy which came from Belgrade which we used to meet on the Bosnian/Serb front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were the factions in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tuzla and that particular area is primarily a Bosnian Muslim area, but we were very close to the Serb front-line so we had some contact with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think in early January, am I right in saying that you actually crossed the front-lines into the Serb-held area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact I went across I think on three occasions, but on one particular occasion, we went down to the area east of Kladanj, which was in Bosnian Serbia, to try and establish links with the Bosnian Serb brigade commander whose troops had been shelling us, or shooting at us, on a daily basis near Kladanj. The aim of that particular visit was to ask the Serbs to stop shelling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you stayed here until February 1993 and then you actually moved back to Vitez in the second week of February, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think here you commanded one of the operations companies, alternating on duty with another company of the battalion, C Company, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities from the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially it was carrying on what we had set out to do and that was to escort humanitarian aid. Our mission had moved on slightly in this time and we were -- we had teams of liaison officers at Captain level who were heavily involved in negotiating with local factions. We were developing routes, carrying out reconnaissance of lots of routes in the area and basically giving a presence on the ground. We were also involved with negotiations with the Serbs to our west in Turbe because they were shelling Travnik, which was of some concern to us, and also because we were quite regularly involved in prisoner exchanges with the Serbs and also, occasionally, body exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have a copy of a map actually and I wonder if the usher could just lift up the first map? For a point of reference, I would like you just to mark on that map the location of the British base in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fine. What is the name of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just south of Stari Bila. It was actually in an old school -- well, in fact it was not an old school, it was a school which had been used up until the time we moved there. We occupied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have marked that with a green pen on exhibit 29. Mr. Registrar, what is the number of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 29H. Thank you. How would you describe the state on the ground, the atmosphere in Vitez, strictly in February of this year; in fact, the atmosphere in the whole of the area of the Lasva Valley where you were patrolling at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did fluctuate considerably. There were occasionally tensions on the ground between the local factions, occasionally roadblocks would be set up by either side to prevent our access into particular areas, particularly if local forces had some sort of operation going on, for example, against the Serbs, but generally the situation was not too bad and we were able to get on with our principal task, which, I repeat, was, of course, to escort humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned the factions in the area. Who were the factions in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They divided up between Croat and Muslim, and they were spread throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown premarked exhibit 100/2 and 100/3 and, for the technical staff, this is Z31 and Z32. First of all, that badge on the screen in front of you, do you recognise that badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is that badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the badge of the HVO or the local Croat forces that we saw in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown new exhibit 100/5, which for the technical staff is Z32; do you recognise that badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the standard army badge worn by all soldiers in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e. the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you regularly see these badges during your time in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that how you actually identified the forces that were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move ahead considerably in time to mid April, and specifically 15th April 1993; am I correct in saying that you went to a small village called Putis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you go to the map that is there in front of you, and if you could mark, actually in a different colour than green, and if you could mark on the map, you are marking in orange the location of the village of Putis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is on exhibit 29H. Why did you go to the village of Putis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say I cannot remember at this stage why we were tasked to go there. It may have been that we were tasked by our own military information cell but the fact was that I was tasked to go there and I went there with, I think, one other Warrior late in the evening as it was getting dark, because we had had reports that the village had come under attack and was threatened. The position was very unclear, so basically I was sent to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who did you meet in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met some local people who were in a very agitated state and summoned me into one of their houses. Putis is only a very small hamlet and they basically implied that they were going to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To which faction did the people of this village belong, the people that were telling you they were going to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they say by whom they were going to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said they were going to be attacked by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the state of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, Putis was a tiny hamlet, just a few houses, nestling in some fairly steep hills. There were just a few people around at that stage. From what I recall, I think they were all men, and basically I had a quick look round the village, I did not have an interpreter with me and there were snatched conversations. One or two could speak simple English and they told me that they thought they were going to be attacked. At that particular time, there were snipers firing in and around the village, so they were basically moving quite quickly from house to house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they frightened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians in the village at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say I cannot recall whether these people were Bosnian army or civilian. I believe they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any women at all in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your professional opinion, how did you regard Putis at the time? What conclusions did you draw about that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation was extremely tense and that they were expecting something to happen. They were not, for example, fortifying their houses or digging trenches or anything like that, but I think they felt they were about to be attacked and they were extremely nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have moved ahead in time from February to April. Can you describe the atmosphere now in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The atmosphere around this particular period in mid April had changed considerably and we were getting reports of various activities going on throughout the area, for example there were various faction leaders kidnapped and shot in Zenica. We were patrolling in Travnik throughout the night, because it was felt that Travnik might erupt into some sort of violence. We were patrolling Zenica, and throughout the whole area there was a significant degree of tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there roadblocks on the roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Erected by both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Erected by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How were you monitoring the situation on the ground? How were you actually receiving information as a regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage our liaison officers had very good contacts with the local forces and the local force commanders. For example, we had a liaison officer in Travnik, we had one in Vitez, we had one in Zenica and we were able to get very good feedback of what the locals thought on the ground, so that was our prime source of information. We also had our own military information cell, which was very well organised and well run and was very good at disseminating information and, of course, from our own patrols on the ground as well as doing our best to escort convoys, we were also maintaining a continuous presence on the ground. We very much felt that something was probably going to happen, but we did not know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to take you now forward to the morning of 16th April 1993. Whereabouts did you sleep on the night of 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in a house alongside the camp and I was sharing a room with Major Alan Abraham, who commanded the 9/12 Lancer Squadron.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was the officer commanding the cavalry component of UNPROFOR in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you awoke at about 6.00 in the morning on that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, we were awoken by enormous explosions, gunfire, mortars going off continuously and quite clearly there had been a major eruption of violence in the whole area so we both reached for our steel helmets and flak jackets and departed in the direction of the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were listening to the sound of this eruption that you have just described. Could you actually distinguish what weapons were being fired by ear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the main weapons were small arms, heavy machine gun, rifle and quite a lot of mortars going off as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say you went to the operations room of the battalion. What is the operations room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was where we had all our -- we did all our planning, we did all our briefings, and where we had all our radio networks, satellite, high frequency, VHF, and it was where all operations on the ground were conducted from. It was where, if you were on the ground in your Warrior, and you were on the radio and you sent a message, that is where the message would go back to, so it was the place where all operations were controlled from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It was sort of the brain of the battalion, as it were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after discussing matters in the operations room, you deployed your entire company into Vitez in Warrior armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially it was my vehicle and I think about a platoon's worth, but then as the situation developed the whole company then very quickly followed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now, please, the usher could place exhibit 56 on to the easel, this is an exhibit that has already been admitted into evidence. Colonel, could you take a look at that aerial photograph? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could stand to one side of it so the judges can actually see it. You say that you went into the town of Vitez on that morning with your entire company. Can you indicate the route that you actually took into the town?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness, he is not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came down the main road, which is coming down this way, the way we always went into town, straight down here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw as you entered the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as we approached the town, it was quite clear there had been a major outbreak of violence. There were a large number of houses that were badly shot up or on fire. As we approached, and I think it is probably the area from about the spot marked "P", up to about probably "O", I think concentrated in the area around about "H" here, we found a number of dead bodies lying in the front of houses and complete carnage throughout that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could take a seat now. So just to clarify, that was the area on exhibit 56 between the letters "P" and "O"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say you saw "complete carnage". Can you describe more specifically exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a large number of houses which had been shot up, in that there were several hundred bullet marks, grenade explosion marks, a number of houses had been burnt out and we found, I think, about a dozen or fifteen bodies on the way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These bodies, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in local civilian attire, shirt, trousers, it was a fairly warm time of the year, and I think almost exclusively, I do not recall seeing any soldiers, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any weapons next to these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What sex were these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, the ones that I saw in the early part of the morning were all male, although we did treat an elderly woman for a gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think various members of the battalion took photographs as you were travelling through from the turret of the armoured personnel carrier. If you could look at exhibits 100/4 and 100/5, which for the technical staff are Z1/232 and Z1/233, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, because I took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise for interrupting, Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The photos we have been provided with, which I assume counsel is referring to, have not been marked in the manner in which counsel is referring to them. They do not have exhibit numbers on them. They have photograph numbers which are different from the numbers counsel is giving to the technical staff, so I just want to understand how we are going to identify the exhibit that is in front of the witness so that we may follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies for that, it is a good point. There is some confusion, the problem is this. The technical staff, in order to show these images from the computer-generated images, have different numbers from the actual exhibit numbers allocated by the court. It is something I have raised, I do not think it is the most prudent way of doing it, but I am afraid for the moment we have to live with it. What I will do as we move along, for the sake of counsel, is actually specifically identify both the number for the technical staff and the exhibit number. I do not believe, Mr. Registrar, that Defence counsel's book of photographs have been marked in the same way as the Registry copy. Is that the reason he does not know what the exhibit numbers are, for the purposes of the court? There is only one copy that has been premarked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, only one of the copies was numbered, but on the list which will be given to the parties and to the judges there will be not only the Registry number but also the number which is on each of the photographs, which will permit us to see exactly what photograph is being used in relation to the number given to it by the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, is this an answer which you can live with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The best answer, your Honour, would be if the unique identifying number on the photograph could be identified at the time the exhibit is referred to, then we can follow along with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then we should say that we all have a photograph in our file here, this is, for example, photograph 232, is that not right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you ask for identification and the witness answers, should you not just say "this is photograph number 232 and then for the technical staff this is another number"? Would that not be a way of working? Would that make it too difficult for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine, Mr. President, that is what I am attempting to do. Unfortunately, trying to remember so many numbers at the same time, it makes it rather difficult, but I will, as we go through each photograph, for the sake of Mr. Hayman and Mr. Nobilo, I will very slowly identify the number both for the court and for the technical staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel can do it quickly, if he just gives us the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the judges, it would also be helpful. Go ahead, please. All right, we are talking about photograph 232. We can start working that way right away and for the technical services this is Z -- what number was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Z1/232 and Z1/233, and the court exhibit numbers are exhibit 100/4 and 100/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the Registry, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a little longer doing it that way, but if it is clearer for the judges and the Defence, then that is how we should work. We would ask the Defence to do the same thing when it identifies documents. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, the photograph in front of you at the time, which is marked 232, what is this photograph an image of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is taken from my Warrior and it is an image of a dead person in his front yard, I suppose, which is typical of many we saw that morning as we drove down that stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If very quickly the technical staff can show 233, which is exhibit 100/5 on the court exhibit numbers, and I think that is the same image taken from the turret of your Warrior, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that you travelled this area and that you saw a number, you say approximately a dozen civilians or persons dressed in civilian attire lying on the ground. Are you aware of the ethnic composition of the persons who resided in this area between "P" and "O"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, this was essentially a Muslim area and as events subsequently confirmed when I was called back there a couple of days later, it was a Muslim area, but, of course, Vitez was split into various pockets of Croat and Muslim, but this area was in the vicinity of the mosque and I know it to be a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How do you know it was a Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we discovered that morning very quickly when we were on the ground that the people that had been killed were Muslims, but also because the fact that we by this stage had been in Bosnia for five months and we knew the area quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you said earlier in your testimony that you came across a female Muslim on the road. How old was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult -- she was probably in her late 50s, early 60s.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could stop there. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask for precision? Lieutenant Colonel, you said that all the bodies were Muslim bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is there any indication that they were all Muslims, or was that your own assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my own assessment, we discovered later that day that they were, and indeed we were involved later, over the days following, in getting some of these people buried. At that particular incident as I was driving along I could not say "that was a dead Muslim", I have to say, but as events unfolded that day and on subsequent days, it was confirmed beyond any doubt whatsoever, there is no doubt about that, that it was a Muslim stretch of road, and as we will probably discover later, I was called back two days later after a bomb exploded and again it was confirmed to me that it was a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Returning to this Muslim lady that you found in the road, what state was she in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had two gunshot wounds; one was not so serious and one was to her chest, which was pretty serious. We gave her some first field dressings and stopped the bleeding and then put her in an ambulance and took her to our dressing station in Vitez camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the initial opinion that you formed as a professional army officer on what had actually happened on that stretch of road? Your initial opinion as you travelled down the road as you saw these dead bodies and the devastation of these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you have to remember, of course, was that this was so unique and so unusual, it was something that none of us had ever seen before and it was not a typical military operation in the sense that we had ever experienced or taken part in. It was something completely different. What struck us all was the ferocity of what had gone on and the fact that there was virtually no limit to what could be done. It was also particularly striking, the sheer level of violence that had been used and the number of rounds that had been fired in the houses to basically clear the people out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any evidence between points "O" and "P" of any defensive positions by a military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any wire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If as part of a conventional operation in the British army we were involved in defending houses for what we call fighting in built-up areas, then there are many ways of doing it with barbed wire, sand-bagging and so on. If you wanted to defend a series of buildings -- there was no evidence that any of the houses in this stretch of road, or indeed anywhere else in the Lasva Valley, were constructed for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then continued on down the road, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you drove past the Hotel Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know what the Hotel Vitez was? Do you know what the purpose of that building was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was essentially the headquarters -- it was part of the headquarters of the Croat forces in Vitez. They had a headquarters across the road from the hotel and the hotel also functioned as the headquarters. Exactly the relationship I do not know, but essentially the hotel was a focal point for Croat forces in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you very quickly point to the Hotel Vitez on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is in the area of "A". It is actually quite difficult to spot exactly, but I think it is "A".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you recall it was in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember seeing anything in particular on that day outside the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was frantic activity throughout the town that day, with cars screeching everywhere and people obviously, in the light of what had gone on, there was a very high degree of tension. There were certainly Croat forces in and around the hotel, but I cannot recall -- I could not put a figure on specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine. Do you recall -- did it appear as if the Hotel Vitez was under attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anybody go into the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not that day, but I suspect, but I do not know, that Colonel Stewart I suspect probably did, or the battalion second in command, or almost certainly some of the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then proceeded on through the town and you went to a Muslim headquarters in Vitez, what you called the Muslim headquarters in your statement, and you spoke to a number of people there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map where the approximate location of that headquarters was, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is slightly more difficult, but I think it is probably in the area marked "B", in that sort of area, but it is quite difficult to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine. So near to the stadium, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the state of this headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had been quite badly shot up, there was a lot of broken glass, there appeared to be some sort of hand-held anti-tank weapons which had been fired at the building. There were several hundred bullet marks in the building and there were probably 10 or 15, I think, Muslim forces in and around the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Light machine-guns, grenades, rifles, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there a commander there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did he say had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation was extremely confused, but they told me they had been under attack and that they expected to be attacked again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the general state of this area of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as bad as the area along the stretch of road that we drove in on, but again large parts of the area had been shot up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "shot up", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By small arms fire, pockmarks of small arms fire in all the walls, broken glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any houses on fire in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Up until this point in time, had you seen any dead individuals that appeared to be soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the Cheshire's -- at this time what was the decided purpose of the Cheshires remaining on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite clearly at this stage our mission of escorting humanitarian aid had changed somewhat and quite clearly we were not going to stand by and let further killing and carnage continue, so what we tried to do as best we could over the next couple of days was put as many armoured vehicles on the ground as possible to try and prevent the local forces killing each other, and also at that time there was a frantic period of liaison, particularly with Colonel Stewart and the liaison officers, to try to broker some sort of peace in Vitez and the surrounding area, but essentially it was maintaining a presence on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And to suppress violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you in and out of Vitez all day that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What I would like you to do now, again as a professional soldier, is to give your opinion on the degree of destruction of civilian objects and property in the Vitez area; if you could describe it to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The worst part of the town was the area I described earlier on, going from the letter "P" up to "O", where there was very considerable destruction and as I said, from the point of view of a soldier, it was something we had never seen before and it was difficult to put into the context of anything we might have experienced, but what clearly had gone on, there had been a very violent attack, probably by a large number of small groups, just because of the scale of the damage, who had attacked houses in a fairly clear-cut way along a stretch of road in Vitez, with a view of either killing or driving people from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the damage that you saw the result of collateral damage caused by the engagement of two military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the fact that the people we saw were civilian, the fact that there were no defended positions in the area and the fact that -- if you were talking about collateral damage you are normally talking about artillery fire and there did not appear to be much evidence of that. What there was was many, many hundreds of thousands of rounds of small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say the people you perceived to be attacked were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it not the object of an infantry force to actually take ground and hold it? Is that the purpose of infantry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is one of the classic, if you like traditional, roles of infantry, yes, to capture ground and to hold it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had this occurred here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because there were no Croat forces occupying the areas that had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what was the purpose of this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to judge, I would assume the purpose was to drive people from their homes and, if necessary, to kill them in the bargain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it an effective operation, could you judge that at the time? Was it possible for you to judge that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was effective, yes. If that was the aim, to get people out of their homes and to destroy them, then it was an effective operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think on 16th April, that evening, you actually slept in the British battalion camp at Stari Bila, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On 17th April you went on patrol, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the usher could now place exhibit 53 on the easel, which again is an exhibit that has been admitted previously. It is an aerial photograph of the Ahmici area. (Handed). Thank you. Colonel, if you could take a look at the aerial photograph on the easel, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly say where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the area east of Vitez, just east of Vitez, starting here probably about one or two kilometres east of Vitez, the village of Santici and Ahmici, and this is the main road leading down towards what we call the Busovaca junction. I will just point out, this is the -- not the main road --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, could you pause for a moment? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This road here is what we call the back road or the mountain road to Zenica, and this is a fairly hilly part of the countryside here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, on this day I think we have already established that you were patrolling in the area, again with a view to suppress violence on the ground and to keep an eye on what was happening, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think on this particular day you were actually travelling on your way to the village of Ahmici, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You had to pass through, did you not, the village of Santici, is that correct, in order to get to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw on 17th April in Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with, I think, one other Warrior, going down the road. As we approached -- I think it was in this area here. (Indicates). There were a number of houses on fire and a crowd of about 35 to 50 refugees were walking down the road, so we stopped the Warrior and jumped out and they were in a very distressed state and pointed to their houses, and were carrying what they had with them and one woman handed me a baby at that time and they were fairly hysterical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did they say to you about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I will be absolutely clear, I did not have an interpreter, but what they said to me was "HVO, HVO" and were basically screaming and shouting and it was quite clear they were in an extremely distressed state. All I could do then was get on the radio, warn off Vitez and got them to warn off the refugee centre in Travnik and point them in the right direction. We then subsequently went over to the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could take a seat now, Colonel. Of this number of people that you have identified, what was the composition in terms of men, women, children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were primarily women, a lot of women, quite a lot of children and a couple of elderly men. There were one or two other men of middle age, but primarily women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they civilians, these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exclusively civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say they were carrying their belongings as they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they leaving quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not running, but they were leaving with haste, on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your judgement of what had happened in the village of Santici, or certainly this area near to Santici, that you have identified on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite clear what had happened. Their houses had just been attacked, literally I think probably 20 minutes or so before we arrived. They were at that time on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there sign of a military engagement between two forces at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any bodies of soldiers, combatants, around on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we found no bodies that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far was this location from the Hotel Vitez, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about two or three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. President, if it is convenient for you, this is a convenient time for the Prosecution to take a break, because we are now moving on to another area of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think in light of what you are going to ask, you are the one who can say what is the best time to stop. All right, I think we can stop now and begin again at 11.35. (11.15 am) (A short break) (11.35 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Can we have the accused brought in, please? (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, would you start from 17th April, that is the part you -- very quickly, starting from that point, 17th April, when the houses were burning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, if there are no objections from the Defence, could I apply for admission of the first five photographs, that is 100/1, 100/2, 100/3, 100/4 and 100/5. As my learned friend has pointed out, they do have different numbers, but for technical reasons. It is the first five photographs in that book that has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection, and I note we are not asking for the source of the photographs to be identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, to recap, as the President has already said, on 17th April, at approximately what time did this event occur, within the environs of Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably about mid morning, about 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you have the microphone on, please, when you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you have already stated, there were various houses burning and you remember a large number of persons actually on the road, actually leaving the village and if you can just -- this may be somewhat repetitious, but just conclude: what did you feel had happened, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe quite clearly we had arrived on the scene just after this small hamlet had been attacked and people had been forced out of their homes violently, although they did not appear to have been murdered -- there was no evidence of people being murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then continued on the same road, past this incident which you had seen. As you stated, you radioed back to Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You told them the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you went down the road towards the village of Ahmici, did you notice anything on the road in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After leaving these band of refugees, nothing in particular, then I turned in up a road towards Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you stand up and identify on the aerial photograph your journey from Santici to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, we found the refugees I think in about this area here (indicates), and I believe that the houses which were on fire I think were in this area. They could have been slightly further up. We then carried on the road going higher. I then turned up this road here and worked my way into Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could take a seat, please, Colonel. Can you describe to the court what you saw on 17th April in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was by now late morning and we were on the fringes of Ahmici and as we drove up a particular track we passed the mosque, which was on its side. I then continued along, we found very many badly burnt out and shot up houses. I then got further up a track and I was quite concerned about the possibility of hitting a mine, so we turned round and then headed back out of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could please look at photograph 100/6, which is marked Z1/171, and if that photograph could be brought up on the screen, please? Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Again, I took this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a photograph of a house on the outskirts of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there many houses in this state in Ahmici when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say you investigated parts of the village to a limit where you thought there might be mines, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any sign of a military engagement having taken place in this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you mean by "military engagement" two forces engaging each other, there was no sign of that. What there was sign of was of a village which had been completely shot up, attacked and burnt out. That is what we saw, but it was not necessarily what you would call a military engagement, it was the engagement of one force against what we subsequently saw were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any defensive positions in the village, any fortified positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any sand bags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any wire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So no indication of any defensive fortifications in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any dead bodies in the village at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on this occasion, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you dismount from your armoured personnel carrier and actually enter any of the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we looked actually in this particular one that the photograph shows, but actually this was only a very cursory look at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see anybody alive in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall seeing -- there may have been the odd person wandering around, but I cannot honestly recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you actually hear any shooting while you were in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense -- not in the village, but all around the Lasva Valley at that time there was sporadic shooting going on, so throughout that period, throughout that period, there was gunfire somewhere and if you looked up into the hills, there were a lot of houses throughout the area smouldering away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now look at exhibit Z1/170, which on the court record is 100/7. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is left of the mosque in Ahmici. The minaret, as you can see, has toppled into the main building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the mosque appear like this on 17th April when you entered the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, again, because I believe I almost certainly took that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How do you think, in your professional opinion, that that damage was caused to that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not a demolition’s expert, but I think it would have been extremely unlikely that that was caused by an artillery shell, because the chances of an artillery shell landing close enough, having been deliberately fired at that minaret, are very extreme. It has almost certainly been caused by perhaps charges being placed around it or even indeed having been set fire to, but as I say, I am not qualified as a demolition’s expert to say, but it certainly is not the result, I would say, of an artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You inspected the houses from the safety of your armoured personnel carrier in the village. Did you actually observe any damage other than fire to these buildings, any damage to the walls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again in common with Vitez, the houses were very badly shot up in the sense that there were many hundreds, in some cases, of bullet rounds, small arms fire and grenade fragments in the houses, more than you would expect just to kill the occupants of a house and drive them out. It was significant to all of us the level of violence that had been used, particularly in Ahmici but also in other areas at that time, the sheer volume of small arms ammunition which was expended was extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again, based on what you have just said, did you reach any conclusion about the nature of this military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at that time, that morning, we were to busy with what was going on to draw specific conclusions as to what had happened. We were more concerned with the now of sorting out people and doing it as best we could. Quite clearly we came to the conclusion that there had been terrific violence used against the occupants of the village. We had not begun to think about the reasons. It was quite clear that people were murdered in their homes and their homes destroyed. The overall reason at that time, frankly, we were not particularly concerned with, it was more the impact of the present, of sorting out the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. If there are no objections from the Defence, I would like to apply for admission into evidence of exhibits 100/6 and 100/7, which are the two photographs we have just viewed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar? They will then be put under which number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers would be 100/6 and 100/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you left Ahmici after viewing the state of the village. Do you remember approximately what time of day this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I am right in saying that you headed towards the town of Busovaca, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly carried on patrolling east down towards Busovaca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there anything in particular that you noticed on the road as you passed down towards the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We always passed at that particular time -- there was a HVO headquarters in the area of -- this area here (indicates) on the left-hand side of the road as you drove down, which was something we called the Alpine Lodge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just point to it once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area here on the bend in the road. (Indicates). It was an area we referred to as the Alpine Lodge, which was a Croat headquarters, and as usual on that particular day there were a number of expensive 4X4-type Shogun vehicles parked outside and some HVO forces, but I would stress that was relatively normal in the sense there were always forces there, but there was activity around those headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Approximately how many people did you see around those headquarters, if you did see anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to place a figure on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember how these individuals were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed as all HVO forces were, with combat kit and small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then returned to Stari Bila camp and I now want to take you forward in time to 18th and 19th April 1993. I think it was whilst you were in the camp at Stari Bila that you heard a very large explosion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was a Sunday evening, getting dark, and we heard an enormous bang coming from the centre of Vitez, and again, as we were at that time the Ops Company, I was sent down -- at that time I went with 2 Platoon, so we went down with about five Warriors. In fact, I was the first Warrior on the scene and we came across a huge explosion, just past the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could pause there, and if the usher could replace exhibit 56, which is the aerial photograph underneath the present photograph on the easel. Thank you. You say that you entered the town of Vitez, you were the operations company, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw when you entered the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
