utterances.text: We came across, in the centre of the road, just past the mosque, the scene of a massive explosion and the remains of what appeared to be a truck or something like that, I think we later discovered it was a petrol tanker, and in the immediate vicinity of the explosion there was a large number of houses which were completely flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the aerial photograph, I know it is marked, the site of the bomb blast, but put where you believe, if you could -- and refer to a letter, the nearest letter to where you believe the explosion took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is in the area between "P" and "H", or it might be further up. It was just past the mosque, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is fine, Colonel, as best as you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been a bit further north, but it was within about probably 100 metres heading into Vitez, past the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the damage that you saw in the town in detail, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, in the immediate vicinity of the explosion, the houses were completely flattened, probably five houses on either side of the explosion, and there were a number of dead bodies as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of casualties that there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we found about five bodies, I think about eight casualties, and then we subsequently discovered, because we then started doing some house searches and about probably 15 minutes after, we found in a cellar a large number of civilians sheltering, they were probably -- it is difficult to remember, probably about 40 or 50 of them at this stage in a cellar, so we got them out and they were saying that they thought they were about to be attacked and they were in fear of their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they say by whom they were about to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not actually remember anybody saying to me "we are going to be attacked by the HVO", but there was only one conclusion to draw because these were Muslims and in fact I know that because we then evacuated them to the Muslim refugee centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the composition of these people in terms of male, female, children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were predominantly women and children and less men, a number of older men. They were in an extremely distressed state, to the extent that I took the decision on the spot to move them out of their houses and move them down to Travnik, so they were prepared at that stage to leave their homes, what was left of them, immediately, carrying nothing and go. That was the level to which they felt that they were about to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So they were very, very frightened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Extremely frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any shooting going on at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was sporadic sniper fire down the main street, but nothing that was particularly untoward for Vitez, although we were quite careful about where we moved. We just backed up -- I then got on the radio and we moved virtually every armoured vehicle we had in Vitez down to the scene and we just backed them up to the houses and put people in the back and drove them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many people did you evacuate to Travnik, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think just over 100, but I would stress at this particular point that at no time, and I was particularly conscious of this on the ground, that at no time did we move any soldiers. It is something that quite clearly I would never have considered doing. It would have been out of the question for me to move any soldiers of either side in a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could look at the final photographs in front of you, which are Z1/246, Z1/250, Z1/251 and Z1/252, the first photograph on the screen in front of you, that shows a Warrior armoured personnel carrier from the Cheshire Regiment, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it shows a 432, a different vehicle, but it is an armoured vehicle from our force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What does this scene depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depicts the area very near the centre of the explosion. You can just see the aftermath there of the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to -- that photograph will be exhibit 100/8 on the court record. If we could now move to 250? Colonel, could you explain to the court what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is looking down Vitez main street and you can just see at the far end of the road remains of the truck and just this side of it, there is a small crater which is where the blast took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of the court record, that will be exhibit 100/9. If we could now have 251, please? What does that depict, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a closer image of the immediate scene of the explosion. Just in front of the gun there you can see where the explosion took place, and further down, you can see the remains of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far had that truck been thrown from the site of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Difficult to say, probably about 100 metres, possibly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What size charge would you need to throw a truck 100 metres down the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not comment on the size, but a pretty big one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That will be exhibit 100/10, and if we can move on the final photograph, which is Z1/252, that I think is a view of the remains of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That will be exhibit 100/11. Finally on this point, there is a very short video clip that I think you can identify of these events, and if the booth could please play that video now? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could make any comments on this, Colonel, as we move through it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a video taken from the turret of one of the Warriors. It is now just driving past the scene of the explosion, which, as you can see, has made a small crater, and then you have the immediate aftermath, as you can see, pretty substantial damage to the immediate houses. It was in this particular area that we -- just a bit further down the street, that we were evacuating that night the inhabitants of the immediate area. (Videotape stopped) MR. CAYLEY; thank you. If there are no objections, Mr. President, from the Defence, I would like to apply for admission into evidence of exhibit 100/8, 9, 10 and 11, and the video clip which I think is exhibit 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then these will be put into the record under the numbers that you have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, if you could now remove that aerial photograph to reveal the map of the Lasva Valley, which is exhibit 29. Colonel, I think a short time after the bomb explosion in Vitez, you proceeded to the HVO headquarters in Busovaca, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you met somebody there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met -- I certainly met a representative from the HVO headquarters who I thought was probably the commander in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. It may have been Kordic, who was the commander there, but I cannot definitely say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you go to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again we had been tipped off, and I think it was through our military information cell or it may have been through the press, who had heard reports there had been some sort of massacre in a village called Kazagici, a village near Busovaca. I was sent off to discover what had gone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you please look at the map next to you and mark on there with a pen, and you are now marking I think with a pink pen, the location of Kazagici, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you have marked on the right-hand side of the map of the Lasva Valley with a pink marker the location of the village of Kazagici. You made your way to the village. Were you able to access the village without any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the bottom of the hill leading up to it, we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom were you stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say I find it difficult to recall. I will not even say, I cannot remember which forces. It was a very confused situation around there. It had been the tail end of a very busy and confusing period. Anyway, we ignored them and drove on up the hill into the village which had been very badly shot up in the style of Ahmici. We did not find any bodies there and the only thing I can remember was a lot of dead cattle. There was then a large amount of gunfire directed at us and in fact I had two reporters from the Daily Mirror with me at that time as well, and in fact we had probably more fire than we had experienced in the whole tour at that stage, personally. We then made our way back to the Warriors and moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the state of the housing in the village of Kazagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it was very similar to one of the exhibits you saw of one of the houses in Ahmici, in the sense they were completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any individuals actually still living in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So there was nobody there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were local forces which we saw around the village, but certainly -- in fact, we walked the length of the village with these reporters and saw nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the last significant event of this particular time you recall was in and around the camp at Vitez, when in fact the battalion itself came under threat, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think there was probably one other event in this period which is the day of the truck bomb, in a village called Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could move on to the events in and around Stari Bila, specifically when the camp itself came under threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end of this particular period, we felt that the camp itself or the houses around the camp, which were Muslim-owned, were going to be attacked. There was a very strong belief by the local people that their houses were about to be attacked by the Croats, to the extent that we put Warriors on all corners of the camp and we started preparing defensive positions, because we believed that the houses in the immediate vicinity of the camp were about to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was there a feeling that you were about to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the houses next to the camp were getting shot at and the local people who lived in them were telling us that they were about to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were the occupants of these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you actually do in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we did, if you like, we doubled the guard, to coin a phrase, but we deliberately put all our Warriors up in the shop window, as it were, and put them on the corners of the camp and prepared, if necessary, to defend ourselves and indeed the people next to the camp. We would not have been prepared to stand by and watch people be attacked in their houses, of whatever side they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there a belief of who you were actually going to be attacked by at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could only have been the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were actually going to attack the base in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think they would have attacked the base, they would have been absolutely mad to attack us, given the armoured vehicles and fire power that we had. I do not think that was on the agenda. I think what was very possible was that they were going to attack the houses next door to the camp and indeed may have attacked or put a bomb or something in the officers' mess, which bordered on the front road. Indeed subsequently, they did attack some of the houses in the sense that one of our interpreters, Debrila Kalaba was shot dead by a sniper just after we left, sitting on the step outside one of the houses next to camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Really this is reaching the end of this period of particularly violent hostilities. In concluding everything that you had seen over those number of days, so after 16th through to about 19th or 20th April, what were your personal views, your personal opinions as a senior army officer on what had actually occurred in the Lasva Valley during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think now with hindsight, it is probably easier to look back and form a judgement than at the time. We were so involved in operations on the ground that we were working 24 hours a day and we were witnessing something which we had never seen before and quite clearly it was very new to us and particularly for some of the younger soldiers, it was very, very different to what they had ever witnessed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you speak more slowly, please, Colonel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What had happened, we were obviously very distressed and quite shocked by some of the things we had seen, but what clearly happened, there had been a massive outbreak of violence in a very short space of time, whereby a large number of civilians had been killed, many of them in their homes, and the level of the violence which had been unleashed on those people was something which was quite striking. There did not appear to be, from our position at the time, any military objective to it, in the sense what we witnessed was straightforward murder in people's houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Looking at the scale of what you saw going on on the ground, was this some uncoordinated bout of violence by disorganised soldiers, or was there any degree of organisation or system that you saw going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what we witnessed was a fairly ruthless and clinical operation, and I say that to the extent that we hardly every saw the events taking place and if we had done, we certainly would have tried to do something about it. Most of the events took place at night, and very quickly and very ruthlessly. One of my platoon commanders did witness in Vitez a small band of men employing, if you like, house-clearing tactics, about to enter a house in Vitez. When they saw him, they stopped what they were doing and then disappeared. I believe that it was co-ordinated in the Lasva Valley. I am quite clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why do you feel it was co-ordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it happened so quickly, because it was so efficiently and ruthlessly done, and because of the fact that we could not actually catch people in the act of doing it. It was quite a clear-cut, efficient operation to murder people and destroy their homes. Also, you know, we were aware of a command structure on both sides. There was quite a clear command structure in the BiH and there was quite a clear command structure in the HVO. We had wiring diagrams, or if you like a family tree of the headquarters of all the organisations. We knew all the local commanders, the liaison officers knew the local commanders. Indeed, if you were moving around on the ground in Central Bosnia and you were stopped at a checkpoint, the first thing that the local commander on the ground would do, very often, if there was a dispute, if we wanted to get to a particular place and there was a dispute, they would get on the radio or the telephone and refer to their higher headquarters. Of course it was a factor, I think probably inherent from the communist system, of clear-cut chain of command and in fact people unwilling to take decisions unless the person senior to them sanctioned it. It was very much a throwback to the old Yugoslav army system or, indeed, the communist system, what we call in the British army a sort of "jobsworthian" attitude on the ground, i.e. "it is more than my job is worth to let you through, I will refer to the person above me". So in that respect on both sides, and I stress on both sides, there was a clear-cut command structure. There was no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You would have had opportunity to compare the quality of the two forces that you saw on the ground, the HVO and the BiH in the Lasva Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you make a judgement during this time of the relative qualities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, the army of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is actually quite difficult to make judgements. What I would say about both sides, particularly when they were fighting the Serbs, and let us not forget that that initially was the main threat, they were brave, dedicated, tough and robust soldiers. I think that equated for both sides. There were many decent and honourable men on both sides. As to make a comparison between the two is quite difficult. I would say that generally speaking, the HVO were probably smarter, probably more efficient and probably slightly better equipped, but beyond that, I would not like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you believe that that plan is in any way connected with the events you saw during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is getting into an area in which I am not particularly qualified to comment. All I will say is I was aware of the Vance-Owen Plan which divided up Central Bosnia into many cantons, depending on the strength of the Croat or the Muslims in those particular cantons as to who governed that area. There is nothing new in this, I, in common with many other people, suspected that what went on might have been a reaction or a preparatory move before the Vance-Owen Plan to cause a population shift in Central Bosnia so that certain sides benefited from the outcome of the Vance-Owen Plan. There is nothing new in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever meet any of the HVO commanders in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not very much and really only in the early part of the tour and indeed very early on, I think in the first couple of weeks in Vitez, we had a dinner night whereby we invited on both sides, Croat and Muslim, commanders from Vitez, Zenica, Travnik into Vitez so that we could meet them socially. So yes, I had met various Croat commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall ever meeting General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I may well have met him, but I do not really remember meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you make any judgement at this time on the quality of the HVO commanders as a group of officers from the British army, did you make a particular judgement at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were aware actually that we were dealing with people that were very dedicated -- of course, in many respects they were fighting against the Serbs, fighting for the survival of their country. They were dedicated professional people, obviously with a different ethos and culture to that of the British army, but I think we had a healthy respect for the commanders on both sides and it goes without saying, and perhaps I should have said at the beginning, as part of our modus operandi as UN forces, we were and remained completely impartial as UN forces throughout our time on the ground. I firmly believe that even during this particular period in late April that we maintained that impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did you finish your service in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we drove out of Vitez on, I think, about May 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You ultimately returned to Germany with the battalion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you were honoured by Her Majesty the Queen for your service in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What award did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MBE.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the Membership of the British Empire. What was that for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mainly for operations that the company conducted in Tuzla in December and January and February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, in effect, escorting humanitarian aid convoys into the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo? I think that one counsel will be enough. If Mr. Hayman is going to do the cross-examination -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is our plan, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just one point, Mr. President, before I conclude, if I could apply for the admission of exhibit 29H into evidence, if my learned friend has no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is the large map, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very good. It has already been filed, I believe, has it not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is numbered and I am going to file it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. How is it going to fit in with the other exhibits that have been put it? Will it have the same number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: When it is a copy of one which has been tendered, we take the same number and add the letter which follows, depending upon the annotation of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Hayman, I am giving you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, Lieutenant Colonel, how are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have had a chance to meet before, have we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were kind enough to grant me an interview in the United Kingdom and we met for some time in connection with that interview, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions. I probably will not finish before the luncheon break but it will not be a very long examination, I think. The BritBat force in Central Bosnia was, had superior armour to any other force in the region, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Namely through your Warriors and other armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did those Warriors also have superior mobile fire power to the other forces in the region, at least the Croat and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What kind of cannon was on the Warrior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30 millimetre cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there also some machine-guns in the vehicle or connected with the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Warrior is fitted with a Hughes' chain gun, which is a machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 7.62 millimetres? What is the size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that the BritBat force had a Mil Info Cell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us first what the function of that cell was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was really to be able to brief all the patrols going out on the ground as to what sort of areas they were moving through, what incidents had occurred in their particular areas, who were the local commanders, the sort of routes they might be going over, problems with bridges, that sort of thing. It was very wide ranging, but it was more, and I stress here, information rather than intelligence. It was to aid -- to make the most of the patrols and indeed getting humanitarian aid around the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By the way, if at any time I ask a question that you feel would be better answered in a closed session without the public and the media, you are absolutely free to make that request and no inference will be drawn from that. Please feel free to let us know if you are uncomfortable with any question I ask in that regard. By what process or processes did the Mil Info Cell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is the Tribunal that makes the decision as to whether or not there will be a closed session at the request of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour. I just want to make sure the witness knows he can ask if he is not comfortable and he should ask if he is uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By what process or processes did the Mil Info Cell gather information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is nothing sinister about this. Basically every time people came back in from a patrol or an escort, they would do a report and hand it in. As I said already, we employed liaison officers on the ground and that was a feature of the way we worked, if you like, classic hearts and minds aspect of putting people out on the ground and they gained lots of information with which they briefed the Mil Info Cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say reports were made when platoons or a company came back in, would that be an oral debriefing or a written report, or would it vary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would vary, but very often it would be a short written report, particularly if there was something new. Very often things were very routine. If, for example, a bridge had been found which could not take Warrior, for example, then that would be reported and it affected the route planning and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, did the Mil Info Cell also derive information from the liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the Mil Info Cell produce a document of its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the Mil Info Cell, along with the operations officer, produced a daily what we call "Sit Rep", situation report of events that day and that would, for example, consist of how many convoys were escorted, the tonnage and what the particular sub-units, for example, the companies, had done that day, but only in very broad outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would the daily Sit Rep -- which I take it stands for "situation report"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The daily Sit Rep, is that the same thing or a different document from a Mil Info Summ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How would you describe the Mil Info Summ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Mil Info Summ was probably a summary -- it was a summary of local force activity, whereas the Sit Rep was more a briefing on -- mainly the aid activities that had been carried out that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the Sit Rep and the Mil Info Summ documents sent up the chain of the command to United Nations, UK land force command or to both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure how far they went, but certainly they went down to Split to our headquarters down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To the headquarters of the UN command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the headquarters of the British forces down in Split, and also, I should add, also to the then UN headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there other regular forms of reporting either within the British forces or to the United Nations that you were aware of, other than the daily situation reports and the Mil Info Summs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from that clearly that were given by commanders, for example Colonel Stewart briefing his superiors at Kiseljak or in Split, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am referring to other written reporting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did you receive information back from the Mil Info Summ so that you would be aware of local situations before you went out on patrol or in some other assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very often, things were so routine that sometimes it was not necessary, but if we were doing -- for example, if we were doing a line crossing, we were for example receiving prisoners from the Bosnian Serb lines in Travnik, a complicated operation which required a degree of security, or something sensitive like that, or we were going to try and approach the front-lines before we went ahead and did something like that, we had a formal session of orders. In that session of orders, a representative from the Mil Info Cell would do part of the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by the term "session of orders"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What would happen, and let us say, for example, that a company was going to conduct an operation to bring back some prisoners across the Serb front-lines, I would sit down with my -- probably with a map like that, with my platoon commanders in front of me, with probably representatives from the ICRC, Red Cross, probably from the UN and other agencies, probably the liaison officers, and we would talk through in a formal way, in which way the British army does its orders, the operation, so everybody is absolutely clear on the structure of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You were the commander of A company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the company keep a company log?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The company did not keep a company log, the battalion kept a log, of which when A company was on operations, there was a log.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe that process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a radio log, A4 size, which sits in the operations room which we described earlier on, and when there is any communication over the radio, the signaller in the Ops Room writes down the message, who sent it, who it was to and the content of the message. It is a way -- it is much less relevant in situations like this, but clearly in conventional war, these things are more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there also such a thing known as the battalion log?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was it really, that was the battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I object at this point? We have spent the last 12 minutes moving through a description of the reporting process of the Cheshire Regiment. This subject is completely outside the scope of questions that were asked in direct examination. We had a meeting for several hours yesterday where we spoke of pinpointing and asking our questions with precision. I do not believe that this is relevant in this examination, and I would ask that counsel be asked to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues for a moment. (Pause). The Trial Chamber has already had the opportunity of taking up this question and in line with what we spoke about yesterday afternoon, the Tribunal is absolutely convinced that the cross-examination must be connected with the principal examination. Having said this, the judges do have faith in the Defence today, as it had in the Prosecution a while back, to understand the theory is respected for a legal and procedural principle. There is a habit which should be taken in this trial, if we want the trial to fit into the time-frame that we have set. Mr. Hayman, this is the desire of the Tribunal, and we will be careful to make sure that things go that way, which means that your questions in your cross-examination must correspond with the questions that were asked during the examination-in-chief. Continue, move on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take that, your Honour, that I may continue my line of enquiry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, perhaps I used language which was not that clear. What we mean is that -- let me try to be clearer, pardon me. The principle that the Tribunal wants to set forth is that the cross-examination must correspond and suit the examination-in-chief. You cannot have a cross-examination, I am saying this to you today and I will say it several weeks and several months from now to the Prosecution, the cross-examination must be fitted in with the examination-in-chief. Having said this, you are the master of your own strategy and it is therefore possible that in the line of thought that you have in the interests of your client that you would sometimes need to move somewhat aside. We do know that the Prosecution had no objection immediately, but waited for about 10 or 12 minutes. Let us be very clear here. The Tribunal wishes that in this Blaskic case, the cross-examination which is carried out should fit in with the examination-in-chief. Having said this, the judges do have faith, and are not going to stop you by saying "you did not follow exactly what the Tribunal had said", because faith in you, up to that point when the opposite party makes an objection, and says therefore that you have to change the line of your question and then move to another line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. If I am being told to stop this line, I would simply note the Defence has not been given an opportunity to be heard as to the relevance of this area. I would note that for the record, that the court ruled without giving the Defence an opportunity to state the relevance, not only to this witness but to the case. I will move on, your Honour. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since yesterday, we have been trying to start with new principles which we are going to set up in a flexible manner. We did not stop you, Mr. Hayman, but we want to assert this principle, that the cross-examination within this Trial Chamber, whether it be yours or the Prosecution's, should be matched to the examination-in-chief. We did not stop you because the principle is to have faith in you, but it is self-evident that if the opposing party objects, the objection is going to be granted, which is what is happening now. If you have two or three questions that you want to ask in order to complete your line of questioning, you can do so, because we are being flexible, but we want the principle to be understood both by you and by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will continue, your Honour. I cannot tell if the objection was sustained or denied. Lieutenant Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I was not clear, the objection was sustained. This is the principle. It is not the Tribunal that stopped you, but given the principle that we have, we are sustaining the objection. As we are now in the process of setting up a principle which to us seems one of good administration of justice, I did not interrupt you immediately, but when the Prosecution objected, we said that this has been sustained. If you have wanted to file questions, then ask them, but in the future, it should be understood that the cross-examinations must fit in with the examination-in-chief, otherwise you understand, as we said yesterday, and everybody understands, otherwise questions are going to be asked of areas that have nothing to do with this, perhaps it would just be to destabilise the witness, today yours, tomorrow the Prosecution's. This would not be part of good administration of justice. This is now a process which is in your hands, but the Tribunal has the responsibility of moving the case forward and the cross-examination must fit in with the examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor's objection has been sustained, but since these are principles that are now being put into place, if you want to ask one or two more questions, go ahead, but in the future it must be clear, I mean clear both for you and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Our position is these are relevant questions and indeed are central to the case. We have not been able to articulate why, but I will move on. Lieutenant Colonel, you stated that there were certain kidnappings of factional leaders in Central Bosnia which escalated or increased the level of tension between the Croats and Muslims in the valley, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that those incidents were very important events in escalating the level of tension in mid April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say how important they were, but they must have been factors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have in mind a particular, as you put it, factional leader who was kidnapped or killed in the days before mid April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not given in my evidence, but I was aware, and I do not recall which side it was, that one or two faction commanders were killed in the Zenica area just before events we described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Commander Totic of the HVO, who was kidnapped in Zenica on 15th April; do you not recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name I do not recall, the incident, as I said, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that some four of his bodyguards were killed, executed in connection with that kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is probably true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that somewhat akin to you or Colonel Stewart having been abducted, in terms of the potential impact on the men under that commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they were fairly senior commanders, I suppose it could have that sort of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Commander Totic was a brigade commander, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there other kidnappings or abductions that you were aware of, for example in Novi Travnik, in the days prior to April 16th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As a result of this increase in the level of tensions, was the BritBat force placed on any kind of alert as of 15th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I explained, we significantly increased our patrolling activity. We patrolled continuously in Zenica during the night, we patrolled in Travnik, certainly. I cannot remember what activity we had in Vitez, because I was involved in Travnik on those particular nights and in Zenica, but I am pretty certain we upped our activity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to mid April, had there been an influx of refugees into the Lasva Valley of which you were aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout our time, there were movements of refugees. Some, for example, came up from Prozor, there were movements of people from Zenica, down from Tuzla; it was a factor of life at that time because so many people had been moved out of the Serb-held areas of Central Bosnia that there were frequent movements of refugees and primarily, we were involved in meeting refugees who had been driven from their homes in places like Banja Luka and meeting them on the front-line in Turbe, so the movement of refugees was a common feature at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there an influx of refugees into the Lasva Valley prior to mid April 1993, insofar as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may well have been. As I said, the movement of refugees was common at that time. There were frequent moves, certainly, of people coming in from the previous Serb areas, so it undoubtedly could well have happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were most of those refugees of Muslim background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have been, if they had come from Bosnian Serb areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that influx of refugees have further increased tensions in the Lasva Valley, tensions between ethnic Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have done, because inevitably if you are moving into an area -- but they were civilians. I could see that tensions could have been increased by the movement of a large number of people into an area. Any country, you know, it is exactly the same, you have a movement of refugees in, it may be a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described for us your visit to the village of Putis. Do you have that in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you went to Putis, you went to see the commander of the Armija in Putis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is in fact who you met with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost certainly, yes. You say the commander of the army in Putis -- there was no army in Putis. Putis was a tiny hamlet and I probably met that night a small handful of people. As I said in my evidence, I cannot recall whether I met civilians or military that night. What I do recall was meeting a handful of people in a hamlet. To say he was the army commander of Putis would be putting the wrong slant on it, because there was no army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The men who you met with in Putis, who you saw there, were they men of able-bodied, fighting age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall the person I met that night was probably in his 50s, but the people that I met that night, the handful of people that I met that night, were male and able-bodied, yes, but they in no way constituted an army or a fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they have any arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, they had small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you were unable to distinguish whether these individuals were soldiers or civilians, or do you believe that they were individuals preparing to defend the village, or engage in some type of military or armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not saying I cannot distinguish between military forces and civilians, what I am saying is I cannot remember on that particular night -- this was at a time of many, many incidents going on on a daily basis and one of many, many patrols that I did. I am being absolutely honest in saying I cannot remember whether they were wearing a uniform or in civilian, but, of course, some of the uniforms on both sides were so civilianised anyway that very often the uniform may be civilian clothes with a badge on it, so you cannot necessarily draw that particular distinction on that particular evening. What I would say is yes, they did have weapons and yes, they were being shot at and I suspect would have returned fire and defended their village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, based on what you saw in Bosnia, that within the army of Bosnia and the Territorial Defence Forces that some soldiers wore uniforms, some wore mixed garb and some wore civilian clothes; would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. The majority wore uniform, there was a lot of what we would call mixed dress and I suppose were little more than local peasant farmers with a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said on the morning of 16th April 1993 you heard small arms fire and mortar fire, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that those are the two most common forms of fire used in fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the situation of Central Bosnia, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As opposed to British army training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would almost certainly use artillery and we may even use armour in the form of tanks as well, but in relation to what the local forces had in Bosnia, yes, small arms fire and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is what you would expect to hear if you were hearing fighting in built-up areas in Central Bosnia at the time, small arms and mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the morning of 16th April, did you hear any sirens going off in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any sirens. I do not recall any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On your drive into Vitez that morning, did you see any HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the initial part, in the area of the mosque and a couple of hundred metres up from the mosque, no, I did not, but as I drove round the town that day -- I was in Vitez for most of that day and I saw soldiers, HVO, mainly around the area of the hotel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On your initial drive into town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but we were going in very fast and quite low in our turrets because of the amount of small arms fire that was going around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So there was still small arms fire in that area, along that strip of houses as you passed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular time, there was certainly small arms fire in Vitez and throughout the day there was small arms fire in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it in terms of the strip of houses, and we will try to find it on the map in a moment to make sure we are all clear what area we are speaking of, but along that strip, you did not see any actual combat between soldiers or soldier and civilian or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we arrived in the aftermath of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you exit your Warrior during that drive in, did you stop at any point and exit the Warrior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not initially, no, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On that initial drive in you did not exit your Warrior at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you turn off the main road on the drive in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on the initial drive in, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we had better find this segment on the map, just for perfect clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps this is where we could break and then start again at 2.30. 19 (12.55 p.m.) (Adjourned until 2.45 p.m.) 22 23 24 25 (2.45 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman -- Mr. Cayley, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is a small point, your Honour. The next witness, I have been reminded by one of my colleagues. Certain protective measures apply to that witness and he just wished me to remind the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Mr. Hayman, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When we broke for the luncheon period, I was, I believe, asking about exhibit 56, the aerial photograph, and I would like to approach and ask you a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I approach the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Again, keeping in mind that the court needs to see the exhibit, and we have a microphone here that you need to speak into, your initial drive on the morning of 16th April into Vitez took you along the path roughly from "P" to "O" on exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that the worst destruction, that is the signs of the heaviest destruction of homes, was around the letter "H" on this map, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the strip "P" to "O", but from what I recall, primarily in the area of "H".

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which is roughly in the middle of this stretch from "P" to "O"? "H" is roughly the mid point of that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This whole stretch along here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were all of the -- strike that. Can you estimate how many houses there were along the road from "P" to "O" on exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Dozens of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dozens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they all on fire when you transited this route on the morning of 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of them were and the great majority had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say a lot of them were on fire, are you saying half were on fire, more than half, less than half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say nearly all had been attacked. Most of them had been burnt out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they all have hundreds of rounds of markings, that is markings from rounds of small arms fire in the walls, or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all of them, but the great majority did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: More than half did, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you shed any light on why some of the homes had so many rounds in the walls and others did not, or for that matter why some were on fire and some were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been that some of the occupants simply were not there, or that some of them possibly may have been lived in by Croats, and therefore were not attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You may take your seat. If exhibit 100, the photo album, could be placed before the witness while I am asking the next couple of questions? During your tour, Lieutenant Colonel, did you learn of any distinctions in appearance between the typical house of a Croat in this region and the typical house of a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Specifically I am asking if you learned whether the roof tops of Croat versus Muslim houses had any differences in them in this area, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you would turn to exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Dubuisson, to fix the microphone. Could you ask the question again, because I do not think we got it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will, your Honour. Exhibit 100/5, which is PH233, do you have that photo before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you see that the roof tops on the houses along the left-hand side of the street would be characterised as two-sided roofs rather than four-sided roofs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But I take it you are not able to tell us whether that is a feature of roof tops that in this region of Bosnia tends to indicate the ethnicity of either the constructor or the occupants of the home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that particular distinction, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in terms of your own experience when you saw the destruction and the casualties in Vitez on the morning of 16th April, you had never seen anything like it, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not surprising, given the scale of what I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, your prior tours had been in relatively -- strike that. Your prior tours had been in areas where there were not open armed conflicts, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My previous operational experience had been in Northern Ireland, so it was a different scenario, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is more of a terrorist war, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had you ever seen fighting in built-up areas, for example, in your tours in Germany, Hong Kong or wherever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I have been on many exercises involving that sort of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about your men? Had they ever been exposed to, for the most part, this type of destruction, if you will, open conflict with casualties and destroyed buildings and the like on this scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had certainly seen elements of it up in Tuzla, when we had been there in January and February, earlier in the year and they had also had experience by this stage of quite a lot of shellfire and shooting, so the platoons had seen quite a lot of operational experience in Tuzla, months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it prior to your and their deployment to Bosnia your platoon or the members of your platoon, to your knowledge, had never fought in a conflict involving fighting in built-up areas, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is they had not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said the houses along the strip of road from "O" to "P" on exhibit 56 were not constructed for Defence, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said they were not fortified for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One moment, your Honour. (Pause). When you now use the term "fortified", you are referring to sand bags, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sand bags, wire emplacements, ditches, that sort of thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that in fighting in built-up areas an important tactical issue is whether a structure itself is being used for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is often a factor. When fighting in built-up areas, very often the defenders will occupy a building and shore up that building to fight from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But they do not necessarily have to shore it up in order to use it as a defensive position, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they do not, but if you wanted to defend it, you would do your utmost to fortify, if you wanted to stay in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you had notice of an impending attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If an attacker learns that a structure is defended, then under the tactics of fighting in built-up areas the mission is typically to clear the house of the enemy, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Including by destroying the structure if necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If necessary, but actually invariably relating to conventional war, if possible you try and leave the structure standing because structures that have collapsed all over the place restrict the movement of your own armoured vehicles. Certainly in our doctrine, we prefer that structures remain standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To do that requires small groups of soldiers moving into a built-up area, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It all depends on the size -- the objective you are taking. You cannot compare a street in Vitez, as you said, a couple of dozen houses, with a major city in Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But a typical assignment for a platoon would be to clear a particular small structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They would do so, would they not, using tools such as grenades, machine gunfire and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is normal if the building is in fact defended, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said it was typical of a fighting force to hold on to territory after it had been seized; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I am referring to conventional operations, that if you have captured ground, you then do not go and leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, though, that the answer to that question depends on a number of things, including where the front-line is; that is, where the confrontation line with your enemy is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be a factor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Namely, if you have been pushed back from the territory that you seized, by definition you are not going to be able to hold it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Or is it possible that an attacker does not have enough forces to hold and occupy territory on a point by point, building by building or even a somewhat broader basis; is that not also possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where was the front-line or the confrontation line on the morning of 16th April 1993 between armed Croat and Muslim elements in and around Vitez, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but there again, the confrontation line changed virtually on a daily basis. The confrontation line varied, depending on which particular command you spoke to. I never saw one confrontation line marked on a map that was the same. In such a fluid situation as this, the confrontation line is virtually meaningless, but not only that, until this particular time, there was no confrontation. This is the point. We were not talking about a battle that had been going on for weeks between Croat and Muslim, up until this particular day -- as we all know, these events happened suddenly, so although there may have been pockets throughout Vitez which were Croat and Muslim there was nothing then regarded as a major confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it fair to say on the morning of 16th April 1993, the confrontation line , such as it was, was dynamic, not static, in and around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The confrontation line changed daily, but there again, the term confrontation line there, you may equate to the Serbs to the west of Turbe, but at that particular time we knew that there were obviously pockets of Croats and Muslims, but there had been no open conflict on the scale that we saw here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that on 16th April 1993, the confrontation line between Croats and Muslims was dynamic, it was moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inevitably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe you said that as you drove along this stretch of road from "O" to "P" on exhibit 56, you did not see any bodies of soldiers, that is dead soldiers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you mean you did not see any bodies wearing uniforms? Would that be more specific and more accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any bodies of people in uniform, correct, but there again I am pretty certain in my own mind, as are my soldiers, that the bodies we saw that morning were civilians. Not only that, but they invariably were the occupants of those particular houses. A number of people we either found in their gardens or, in two cases, draped over their fence. If they were soldiers, they were spread out far and wide and you would expect to find groups of them, if they had been defending a house. You would not have soldiers defending one person per house, so it very much gave the impression that these were the civilian occupants of these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If a soldier is off duty, are you referring to them as a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he is off duty, he is still a soldier. But what I am saying is the people in the houses we saw were wearing civilian clothes and I deemed to be civilians. What reinforces that particular point is the fact that when I extracted, I think on the evening of the 18th, people from along that street, as the point I made quite clearly, I insisted that night that we carried no Bosnian army soldiers in any military vehicle and every person we moved out of that location, which was in the same street, was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe you said of the 12 bodies or so you saw between "O" and "P", they were all male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, yes, that was the case. As I said, we treated one elderly woman for a gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The bodies of males that you saw, were they roughly between the ages of 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although one of my platoon sergeants, Sergeant Kujvinksi, in a well-documented account, recalled seeing a boy of about eight years old dead, cradling a puppy that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you say you did not go into any of the homes along the strip of "O" to "P" on that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not initially, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Later in the day, did you go into any of the homes, on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So if there had been shell casings or other signs of defence within any of those homes, you would not have been in a position to discover it on the 16th, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you came to the Hotel Vitez on the morning of 16th April, did you exit your Warrior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall doing so, because on that particular morning, the battalion second in command was also on the ground in his Warrior and I am pretty certain he went to the Croat headquarters. I personally did not that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That would have been Major Waters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you tasked to go to the Armija headquarters in Vitez, or did you do that of your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did that of my own initiative. As I said, at that time pandemonium had broken out throughout Vitez. There was continuous gunfire and we were just doing our best to establish just exactly what was going on. At one particular time I ended up at the Armija headquarters, but it was of my own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You identified that the Armija headquarters at point "B" on exhibit 56; are you comfortable with that location as your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said at the time, I am not entirely comfortable with it, no. All I said was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we have the microphone on, please, and if you could slow down a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not absolutely comfortable that was the location. I believe it was in this general area here, but we are dealing with a small air photograph and that was the first time, that morning, I had been to that headquarters. I think in that area is probably specific enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the general distinction between Vitez town and Stari Vitez, or old Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this headquarters that you went to in Vitez town and not in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Vitez town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, you may have a seat. Can you give us an estimate how far this headquarters, that is the Armija headquarters you visited, was from the Hotel Vitez within Vitez town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give an exact estimate, because I was slightly unclear as to the exact location. It would be wrong of me to give an exact distance, but it would be no more than a mile and no less than half a mile. That was the sort of distance. It is a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the outside of the Armija headquarters in Vitez looked, so to speak, "shot up"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Inside there was a military commander with approximately 15 soldiers, armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I need to call your attention back to exhibit 56. Would you expect, in an armed conflict, between two armed forces, that the worst devastation of, for example, structures where fighting in built-up areas occurs would be in and around the front-line, that is, the confrontation line between those two forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would expect probably the heaviest fighting to be where the opposing forces first engage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is because if one takes a structure and the other side takes it back, in the course of all that fighting, the structure is likely to show very significant signs of battle, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the strip of the stretch you have described, going roughly from "H" to "O" in fact represents the area very close to if not the front-line or confrontation line between the Armija and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must be close to what you are telling me is the confrontation line, but as I said, I do not necessarily believe that is the right definition. It was certainly -- that stretch of road was an area which at one point divided Croat houses and Muslim houses, certainly. But there were pockets throughout Vitez and that is why the confrontation line is so difficult to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With the court's permission, I am going to place over exhibit 56 an overlay which has previously been marked and admitted as exhibit D26, an overlay marked by another witness. Let me ask you, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas, I will ask you to stand, you see on this overlay which we have placed to match up to the legend and so forth, so it is in the proper location, we see a red outline roughly around the area of Stari Vitez, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you also agree that parts of that line representing the area within Stari Vitez and dividing it from the area outside Stari Vitez are virtually at point "H" on this map, exhibit 56, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that other parts of it run along the road that reaches from "P" to "O"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I would say that this -- I mean, this scrawl on here is virtually meaningless. The thing is, as I said, confrontation lines vary between who drew it. I have seen many similar maps to this and the fact of the matter is these lines do not necessarily mean very much. I do not believe this actually can be regarded as a tactically significant overlay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you mean by that -- I will allow counsel to return to his place. Do you mean by that that the presence of an army of BiH soldiers in Stari Vitez was not of strategic significance to the conflict between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure the presence of troops must have been significant and I do not dispute that. Of course the presence of BiH troops must be significant. However, that does not necessarily conform to what you are saying there. What I have said consistently is that that morning I saw no dead BiH troops and that is a fact. What you are saying is that somewhere within this confrontation line there was a pocket of BiH troops. That may be the case, but I did not see any. Not only that, but the validity of this confrontation line I would question anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did not see any troops at all in that area of Vitez, Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw no dead troops; indeed, I saw no live ones, apart from the ones I saw at the BiH headquarters, primarily, and then throughout the day the odd individual in the odd house, spread throughout the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that there were BiH troops on 16th April in Stari Vitez, in some numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to April 17th. You were driving, I believe, on the main road from Vitez to Busovaca in the direction of Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you saw a number of refugees on the road, perhaps 30, perhaps 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you saw houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were those houses on the south side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were on the right-hand side of the road as you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As you look at exhibit 56, they are on the right-hand side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they the houses immediately adjacent to the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones I saw on fire were probably about 100 or 150 metres from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they the first row of houses next to the road or were they several rows back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is extremely difficult. They were in a patch of open land, I think about 150 metres from the road. They were very clearly visible from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They would have a commanding view -- a line of sight view of the road, correct, from those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a commanding view, they were just near the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were higher than or as high as the road, or were they below the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area around there is pretty flat, and they were virtually on the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
