utterances.text: During your tour, did the army of BiH ever cut that road in approximately that position, or was that after your tour ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was after our tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you did not see any fighting in this area as well, you saw refugees and houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You saw no soldiers in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is the same true in Ahmici when you turned up the road to Ahmici on the 17th, you saw no fighting and no soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you go in any homes to look for evidence of possible defence, such as spent shell casings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph you saw as one of the exhibits there, I went into that particular house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Referring to exhibit 100/6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am holding up for the record, your Honour, 100/6. That was the only house you went in on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you go out from the area of the road to look for any possible fortifications, such as a trench or a fox hole or something of that sort, or did you stick to the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stuck to the road because of the fact that the mine threat was quite significant and I was not prepared to risk the Warrior on a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that there was in fact a headquarters of the Armija and/or the Territorial Defence in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you make a report of your visit to Ahmici on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have certainly got on the radio and told the company headquarters what I was doing, yes. I do not recall writing a formal report of that particular recce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that because in the context of the conflict and the destruction that you were seeing, Ahmici did not stand out particularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not stand out that morning, but, of course, later on my 1 Platoon, under Lieutenant Dooley, actually discovered what is now known as the massacre in Ahmici, and it took on much greater significance. The part of the village that I was in did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you completed your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it on the morning of 17th April when you went into Ahmici, in fact went in one building, one structure, you were not aware there had been a massacre in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that stage, I do not think, no. As I said, I saw no dead bodies at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had you heard from any other BritBat soldier or BritBat source that BritBat forces had been in Ahmici on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have done, because it was my company that were the Ops Company at the time. This is where I am unclear on the chronology of this, whether or not Lieutenant Dooley -- the exact period when Lieutenant Dooley discovered the massacre in Ahmici. I may have been in that particular house the day after Lieutenant Dooley discovered the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But when you were there on the 17th, were you thinking "this is where a massacre of 100 people or more has occurred", or was that not in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But in any event, you made no special report or written report of your visit on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall doing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to 18th April 1993, and the truck bomb in Stari Vitez. You were one of the first UNPROFOR officers on the scene. Did you gather any evidence from your visit that would tend to shed light on whether the truck bomb was essentially a terrorist act or whether it was a military operation sanctioned at a high level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is impossible to draw that distinction. As I said in my evidence earlier on, at that particular time all we were interested in was sorting out the people on the ground as best we could. To draw distinction whether it was a terrorist act or part of some campaign plan was not really a factor. It was, if you like, a terrorist act as we know it, but in the context of a localised conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But I take it you did not gather any evidence through forensic or other sources or your Mil Info Summ tending to indicate who had directed that attack, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could only surmise the fact that it was just down the road from the mosque, that it was in the area we knew to be the Muslim area, therefore we surmised it to be targeted at the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By some Croat element, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any Armija soldiers killed as a result of the truck blast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies pulled out of collapsed buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were any of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any arms, that is guns and the like, taken out of any of those collapsed buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, or not that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any arms taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Some time later you went to Kazagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there soldiers in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers not in the village because we were able to walk through it without seeing anybody, but as I said in my evidence, around the village there were a number of local forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of the same side or of different forces, or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, at the bottom of the hill, and this was where I was not clear in my earlier evidence, because I could not specifically remember. At the bottom of the hill leading up to Kazagici, I believe there was a Croat checkpoint which we drove through. Around the village of Kazagici I think there were BiH soldiers, but I would not wish to swear on that. All I am saying is the village of Kazagici, and I have no doubt somebody here in the Tribunal would be able to ascertain whether it was a Croat or a Muslim village, all I am saying is that particular village had been completely destroyed. I am not interested whether it was Croat or Muslim, it was a terrible act. All I am saying is the village was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From what you have described, do you think it sounds like that village was at the confrontation line between Armija and HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably close to the confrontation line, again a difficult term, because of the sheer level of gunfire that was in and around that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell whether that gunfire was directed at you or whether it was being exchanged between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of it was definitely directed at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your earlier testimony that attacks in the area of the Lasva Valley in mid April happened so quickly; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How long did the fighting go on after it began on the morning of the 16th? Did it not go on for a period of days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of days, and in villages in and around Vitez there were battles for a longer period than that, but the main fighting in Vitez and Ahmici and so on was up and over in a period of a day or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you said "so quickly" you meant in many instances a day of fighting or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not even that. There was sporadic shooting over that period, but the instances we have been referring to in Ahmici or the attack in Vitez happened in the space of a couple of hours, because, as you know, we woke up on the morning of the attack on Vitez, I think the 16th, and everything had happened in the space between going to bed that night and 6.00 in the morning, so probably a period of six hours, a whole street in Vitez was flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But the fighting woke you up on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it was not going on between midnight and 5.00, it started at 5.00 or 6.00 am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And then you responded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You started to describe your visit to Cajdras, but you were not able to elaborate. Do you recall roughly when that visit occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That visit was on the day of the truck bomb, which I think was the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Roughly where is the village of Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the hills south of -- a few kilometres south of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: North of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: North of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you went to that village, who did you encounter? What type of force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I encountered a group of Muslims who had been -- who appeared to have ransacked some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, I have not objected before, there have been a number of points where I was going to object, but in order to get through matters -- but at this point, we do wish to make a very strong objection. Defence counsel is now seeking to introduce evidence of potential breaches of international humanitarian law committed by another faction, in this case Islamic extremist forces. The Prosecutor's position on this is that this is a fundamental question. It is a fundamental question for the following reasons. Alleged crimes committed by other parties are irrelevant to the case before you. They are not contained -- the village of Cajdras is not referred to in this indictment and indeed, General Blaskic, it is not alleged that he had absolutely anything to do with these events at all in this village. This document sets out the four square corners of this case. The fact that another party committed a crime is not a defence to General Blaskic. Thirdly, the matters to which counsel refers may well be the subject of a separate investigation by the Office of the Prosecutor, and public revelation of those matters may well be prejudicial to such an investigation in its nascent stage. Lastly, and a matter which we addressed yesterday in the status conference, the raising of these extraneous matters consumes precious time of the court, it delays the course of justice and it ultimately distorts and bewilders the truth, which after all, I would respectfully submit, is why we are here, to find the truth. For these reasons, I would respectfully submit to the court that both the Defence and the Prosecution be precluded from asking questions of alleged breaches of international law which are not the subject of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I give the floor to Mr. Hayman. I would just first like to point out, I have not decided about the objection, but I would like to know whether this was -- the Colonel did mention this, did he not? So on the basis of the principle that we will indicate that the cross-examination has to be part of the examination, he did mention it, but your objection raises other problems and I would like first to give the floor to Mr. Hayman so he gets his opinion -- gives his opinion on what was just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course defence counsel must have his say, but I have one other point to make. The Colonel did actually mention the name of the village. He did not get on to the subject-matter, because it was my view that it is not relevant to this case, for the reasons that I have given. I will not repeat them. So the actual subject matter of this event was never raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. I could not agree more with the principle that crimes committed by other persons, other parties, are not relevant of and in themselves, to this case. But that is merely the beginning, not the end of the inquiry. The question is: did the presence of Mujahedin, call them soldiers, call them terrorists, what you will, on the soil in Central Bosnia, is it relevant to the level of tensions between Croats and Muslims? Is it not relevant much in the same way the kidnapping of Commander Totic and the execution by, it is believed, Mujahedin fighters of his four bodyguards are relevant to understanding the conflict, what gave rise to it. That is one area of relevance. The other is this witness has testified to very broad opinions about the causes of the conflict, the nature of the conflict, et cetera, and I think we have to be allowed to probe. If it is confidential, the last thing we wish would be to contaminate any such inquiry, but we submit it could be done in closed session with no danger of any such contamination. By the way, I have three or four questions in this area. It is not time consuming. I would have been done long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I rather tend to some extent to agree with Mr. Hayman. I will explain why. I want to limit as much as possible the examination and cross-examination, but the case does not -- the judge does not have the entire case file, so he cannot criticise or tell either of you what to do. It seems to me, however, just as I will ask Mr. Hayman not to dwell too long on this point because it was only mentioned by the Colonel, I do believe that it is actually natural for General Blaskic's Defence to show, as much as he can, a possible, if you like, mitigation of responsibility of his client. Have faith in us, Mr. Cayley. If the questions having to do with this climate that reigned go on too long, I believe we would be the first to stop Mr. Hayman. But I think that we cannot prevent the Defence from trying to characterise what this climate was. We are not saying that the village was far away, it was a village -- that it was very far away, hundreds of kilometres removed from the combat area. I would be the first in that case to say absolutely not, you cannot ask questions about that, but it is true that the Colonel mentioned it, I even noted it, the name was in the Colonel's mouth and he said it. So I am very strict about what has been said and I think the cross-examination has to remain within the limits of the examination-in-chief. He did mention it, the Colonel, that is, we can understand that the Defence might be used to support his Defence in one way or the other. Therefore, Mr. Hayman, go ahead, but do not spend the whole afternoon, please, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I should be done within half an hour with my entire examination, your Honour. Lieutenant Colonel Thomas, you went to Cajdras, you encountered a group of Mujahedin fighters; about how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not saying they were Mujahedin, because I cannot categorically say they were, but what I will say is they were a particularly aggressive group of Muslims who I had not encountered before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they bearded? Were they wearing beards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, they may have been. But they were Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you put a rough number on the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were probably about six or eight of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did they, if anything, do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not get my Warrior very close because it was on a very steep hill, so I walked forward with my Sergeant Major and a female interpreter. I asked them what they were doing and I asked them to stop. They looked like they had been looting houses, there were some wrecked houses there. I asked them what they were doing. They refused to talk to my interpreter and became very aggressive. One of them put a grenade under my chin. I thought it was probably best that we leave with a degree of dignity and we walked back to our Warrior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He physically put a grenade under your chin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you see houses burning -- how could you tell houses had been ransacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not burning at this stage. I stress this was not the village of Cajdras, this was a tiny hamlet on the top of a hill of probably three or four buildings near Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On what do you base the statement, just in a general sense, that the houses were being looted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were obviously working their way through the houses. The houses were not burning but they had been ransacked and shot up. I think what I would say is the reason I was -- perhaps against the wishes of the Prosecution -- that I was even keen to put this in evidence was that I believe it showed our impartiality in investigating claims by in fact the priest in Cajdras, a Croat priest, that there had been a problem there, which I would hope puts my other evidence in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You and your men had difficulty at times moving through Croat checkpoints as well as army checkpoints, is that in part what you are saying, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At all times when there was tension we had difficulties moving through checkpoints, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before your testimony, did you have occasion to review any radio logs of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Including the watch keeper's log?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether you were interviewed, anyone reading from any of those logs as part of your preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is to your knowledge no one did, no one was referring to a radio log in the course of interviewing you or preparing you for testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that in fighting in built-up areas most of the fighting is done by small groups of soldiers, platoon or smaller?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normally -- again, it all depends on the level of war you are talking about. Individual houses are attacked by small groups of people, but normally, such operations are done in conventional war by battalions and brigades, who then break down to clear individual streets and houses. In the case of Vitez, I imagine that a fairly large force broke down into small bands and attacked houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that type of fighting make command and control more difficult, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Command and control is inevitably difficult in FIBUA, but you normally work -- the thing about FIBUA, Fighting In built-up Areas, is that you worked to a very detailed plan and such operations are planned in minute detail, normally with air photographs and individual platoons and sections being detailed the houses that they should take on. Although during the actual operation the command and control may be difficult, although not impossible, the planning for a FIBUA operation is normally conducted in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that proper planning for such an operation requires training and rehearsals and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the British army was conducting such an operation, it would carry out rehearsals, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One moment, your Honour. (Pause). Your Honour, I have three or four more questions, but I think they are most appropriately asked in closed session and I can explain why, but probably not outside of closed session. I can write it down in a sentence or two if that is convenient, as the court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we havea closed session, I first would like to turn to the Prosecution. Do you have any objections to a closed session, since these are questions which would involve a certain number of secrets?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The problem is, Mr. President, I have absolutely no idea what the questions are, so I cannot make any objections. Clearly the only way we will find it is if we go into closed session. I have no objection to a closed session. That does not mean to say I will have no objections to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will now have a closed session and then if we have to get out of closed session once again, we will decide that. For now, we will have a closed session, unless you want to have something absolutely in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think if we just turn off the sound, that is enough. We need not lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If we cut the sound, that is enough. That is fine. We will cut the sound. You do not have to turn to any maps or anything like that. You are sure? We do not have to draw the curtains. We will simply say that this is now a private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Page redacted in closed session Page redacted in closed session page redacted in closed session page redacted in closed session page redacted in closed session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Lieutenant Colonel Thomas, a couple more questions. You said that the HVO, in your view, had a "clear command structure".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe you said you based that on, for example, individuals at checkpoints calling their commanders before making a decision whether to let you pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Typically what commander would a guard at a checkpoint call in order to confer on that type of matter, if you know? Would they call their commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The local village platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or often physically go and get him and bring him down to the checkpoint as well. This could sometimes take half an hour, it could even -- it sometimes could take hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any basis for testifying before this Tribunal concerning the nature or the strength or weakness of the command structure of the HVO at the top level, at the upper levels? What you have described is the bottom of the ladder. What about at the top, do you have any basis to give an opinion there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on the basis that we, certainly our Mil Info Cell was very clear on the names and structure of the hierarchy and it seemed fairly settled and unchanging in the time that we were there on both sides. It was not fluctuating, and we knew where to go at all times, and certainly Colonel Stewart and the liaison officers always knew where to go to find the commanders. There was a fairly settled command structure on both sides and we could, with a good degree of confidence, draw a line explaining the hierarchy of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What I am asking is, do you have a basis to testify whether or not the command structure at the upper and mid level range, did it work, was there command and control? Were orders uniformly followed, or do you not have a basis for testifying on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a basis for saying they were not uniformly followed. From our dealings on the ground, people tended to do as they were told and at some particular checkpoints when life was particularly sensitive sometimes we were stopped going through at all and people were very robust, because their commands had told them. I think generally on both sides there was a reasonably effective command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But your personal experience was in the main at the checkpoint level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I had dealings in Tuzla, for example, with the Bosnian Muslims, I had dealings with the Serbs and with the Croats throughout my time at all levels and I believe that there was a reasonably strong command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What example can you give us on which you would base testimony, if you are so testifying, that the command and control exercised at the top of the HVO was, for example, commensurate with the type of command and control that exists in the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not trying to establish and never have done that the command and control of the HVO is commensurate with the British army, and that has never been said. What I have said is we were able to quite clearly work out a wiring diagram, there was no secret to that, and we knew the commanders and we had to know the commanders anyway to open up certain routes. There were certain times, for example, opening up routes in and around Vitez where we needed the permission of the local commanders. That was often granted or not granted, in and around Maglaj, for example. We had to go to commanders to get clearance to go up certain routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But again, you are talking about clearance to get through checkpoints to deliver aid and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very often these were very sensitive issues, because they were near the front-line, so, you know, it is not necessarily taken by the chap down the road who is the local boss. Some of these were relatively high level issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you involved in trying to gain the enforcement and implementation, for example, of cease-fires, or was that something you were not involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not involved in that directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are there other operational areas other than aid convoys and getting through checkpoints where you had actual involvement and you could base an opinion of the type that I am asking about, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My main dealings at that level were at core level in Tuzla and I had a number of negotiations with the core leadership regarding the movement of convoys across Bosnian Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the higher level, your direct dealings were limited to the army of BiH in Tuzla, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I also had dealings with various Croat commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Brigade commanders or lower level commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have a substantive meeting with General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know his headquarters, his headquarters staff and how it functioned, or did not function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you went to Maglaj. Did you deliver or escort aid to Maglaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Maglaj on several occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was aid delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that aid transported by an aid or relief organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It varied. Usually, from what I recall, it was transported in UN trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Under UNHCR auspices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that aid delivered to a warehouse -- to whom was it delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I am pretty certain there was an UNHCR warehouse in Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that as far as you would see it go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were not responsible for the door step delivery of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a significant civilian population in Maglaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maglaj was a fairly significant town, primarily because of its proximity to the Bosnian Serb front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it mostly populated by army of BiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a mainly Muslim town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it mostly populated by soldiers, not civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, and I would not like to give the impression, because it would be very wrong and false, that we would be delivering aid to BiH soldiers. That was never the intention of the UNHCR and something we would desist from doing. As I have stated all along, our impartiality was absolutely crucial to our success. There may have been BiH soldiers in Maglaj, there may have been Croat soldiers elsewhere where we delivered aid. The decision to take aid to Maglaj and other locations was the UNHCR's and not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas. Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor wish to rebut anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, Mr. President, to confer with my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may. (Pause). Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Mr. President. I will be as quick as I can. Colonel Thomas, in your cross-examination you said to Mr. Hayman that prior to 16th April 1993 there were no confrontation lines in Vitez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I think the term "confrontation line" is perhaps a misnomer, because there was no real confrontation. The town was split up into factional areas, but the term "confrontation line" I am not sure was applicable at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So although there was tension, there was no fighting between -- no higher intensity fighting between the parties prior to 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on the scale that we saw -- that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One last question: all of the events that you observed over that number of days, approximately between 16th and the early 20s of April, so about 20th April, at the time, did you reach a conclusion whilst you were in Bosnia about the nature of this attack, in its totality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the brutality and the callousness of what we witnessed I think was our biggest abiding memory and I think the conclusion that we reached was that we had witnessed something of a ferocity and a viciousness that is almost impossible to describe. What I believe we witnessed was an attack by and large on civilians in Ahmici and in parts of Vitez, to drive them from their homes. For whatever reason, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to now turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad, have you any questions you want to ask the Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel Thomas, I would like to ask you a few general questions of a general character, and the answer came to me through your answers both to the Prosecutor and to the Defence, but still I might like to have more precision. You mentioned several times, just the last one was right now, that there was a mass of ruthless violence unleashed on the people without any military objective, as you said now, unleashed on civilians. You cannot tell us more about the purpose of this unleashing of ruthless violence? If it was not a military objective, what was the objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well sir, because of the very local nature of the conflict there, if we were referring to conventional war, one could argue you would capture a road or a hill or a town which would have some tactical or strategic significance. The fighting in and around Vitez was so sporadic and localised, it was difficult to define any tactical or strategic reason for why things happened. That is why I am inclined to the belief that it was out of sheer viciousness and hatred that people were driven from their homes in certain streets and certain factions, because it was actually quite difficult to define any strategic objective. I do not know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I gathered from your testimony too that it was not haphazard action, there was some kind of organised and co-ordinated acts going round. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think to succeed with the speed that the forces did succeed, in the number of areas that they operated in, I think there had to be some sort of co-ordinated plan. I do not think you could have destroyed so many houses in Ahmici and in Vitez without some sort of co-ordinated plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those who committed these acts, not to speak of those who made the plans, were they military or paramilitary or simple civilians, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think going back to my last answer, I think to carry out such an -- almost a Blitzkrieg-type assault on those houses, in arguably a successful way, would indicate that they were military forces with some sort of co-ordinated command and control structure. I cannot see that it was the work of disaffected locals or villagers of a different faction suddenly deciding one night that they were going to kill their neighbour. The scale and the brutality in that valley would indicate it was something much wider than just disaffected former friends who had been living side by side deciding one night to kill their neighbours and burn their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As I said, it was the act of some kind of military groups. Putting this in perspective with your explanation of the chain of command, which you tried to describe as a result of the communist system, it was -- I even can quote you somewhere here, you said: "It was deference to the person above and a clear-cut chain of command." Nobody almost was ready to take decisions on himself, always had to refer to others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In that case, do you think the military committing these acts committed them with their own free will or had to refer to superior orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the individuals who were responsible, for example, for murdering families in their cellars in Ahmici, must have been ordered to do it by somebody. They did not do it of their own free will. I think they were operating under orders from some sort of wider plan, whatever that plan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: All those murdered, was there among them Croats too, or the houses demolished and burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure there were, and again I stress our impartiality. Amongst those people that were murdered in and around Vitez in the Lasva Valley there were undoubtedly Croats, but I have been referring to the incidents of the truck bomb, Ahmici and that particular strip of houses in Vitez where the great majority were Muslim. I carry no torch for either side, I am merely reporting what I was asked to and what I saw on those particular days. There were Croats killed, but the majority of people in the incidents I have been asked to describe were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Croats killed live in Muslim areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My last remark was concerning the refugees. You said there was a movement of Muslim refugees coming from the Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were these refugees aggressive, did they represent any imminent danger to the population, to the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. These were people, and I was involved in several operations to escort refugees across the front-line west of Travnik at Turbe, and these people were completely downtrodden, carrying their possessions in plastic bags. The last thing they were was aggressive. They had nothing. They had no future. They were not aggressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel, just a few questions. I understood you to be testifying that you spent around five months in and around the Lasva Valley area, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit less than that, sir, because I spent about a total of seven or eight weeks in either Kladanj or Tuzla, so really about four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: About four months then. I stand corrected. During your tour of duty, you were given information about the main military aspects of the armed conflict in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were certainly given lots of information, sir, but, of course, at this particular time, through most of our tour, our main concern was surrounding Bosnian Serb movements, particularly as regards Vitez, to the west of Vitez. For example, we were concerned that the Serbs may try and shell Vitez, because it was in range.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What I mean is, did you become acquainted with the main elements of the military situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understood you to be saying that in the Lasva Valley area there developed a problem between two sides, Croats and Muslims, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You yourself were not involved in negotiating any cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you served in BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was BritBat involved in negotiating any cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. At the time, after this period of 16th to 18th April, there were attempts at localised cease-fires, but the negotiations were conducted at a higher level, mainly with Colonel Stewart and the liaison officers because, of course, this is an extremely serious outbreak of violence. I was really more a player on the ground with my armoured vehicles. The negotiation level was done by Colonel Stewart, but there certainly were BritBat negotiations to try and establish some sort of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those negotiations would be conducted as between what military elements on each side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have been conducted between Colonel Stewart, various liaison officers from the ECMM and possibly UNHCR, and I suspect representatives on both sides at brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say both sides --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the HVO and the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you told us of the character of the military command structure on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it your impression that there were operating on either side any military units which were totally independent of the two command structures which you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a possibility that there were extreme elements on both sides that were capable of operating independently, but I did not come across any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You did not come across any. Now, the assessments which you made as a military officer of the incidents to which you referred on 16th April and 17th April would have led you to what kind of conclusion as regards the possible involvement of independent military units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose there is a possibility that independent units could have come from outside to carry out those acts, but I think we would have probably noticed the movement of forces coming in and indeed leaving, if they were going to carry out those acts. But beyond that, I cannot say, nor would wish to, who did them. All I can say is the evidence I have given already, that I believe they were carried out by an organised force operating with a coherent command and control structure, operating to a certain plan. I do not believe they were some renegade element. They may have come from outside; that, of course, is a possibility, but I think unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You saw any evidence of their participation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You got periodically, I imagine, information from Mil Info about the command structure on either side and the distribution of forces, I would suppose. Did your dealings with people and organisations on the ground tally with the information which you got from Mil Info about the command structure on either side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I think Mil Info was fairly accurate in its descriptions, because again, really up until this time, we were not too worried about the command structure, because there had been no real conflict, so there was no great secret as to who was the various commander in each location and so on. It was open knowledge, the BiH and HVO structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel Thomas, I just wanted to add one question to see things more clearly in your answers. Was the HVO in full control of these areas where these acts were committed, or was it a no-man's land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know I can give you a clear answer to that, sir. I think Vitez was a mixture of HVO and BiH before 16th April and before then, I could not say that the Croats or the BiH were in control of it. I think after 16th April the HVO certainly had the upper hand. With regard to Ahmici, I really cannot say who had the upper hand before. It was a Muslim town or village, I assume that obviously therefore the BiH ran it -- not necessarily ran it, but certainly the Muslims there were obviously in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am speaking of the areas where the acts you mentioned, burning houses and seeing the corpses, killed, these very specific areas where the acts were committed, were they controlled by the Muslims, Serbs, Croats or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Ahmici was a Muslim town, or was. It was controlled by the Muslims before the attack on it. The strip that I have been referring to in Vitez which was attacked was a Muslim area of Vitez which was largely controlled by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then why did the Muslims not defend it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is the whole point, sir. They did not defend it because it was not a military target. They were simply the homes of people that lived there, so therefore, and this is really the crux of the argument, it was not a military installation or a military sector or an objective -- this goes to the point why it was not defended, because there was nothing to defend. It was merely a strip of residential houses that were lived in by Muslims. That goes down to the point that none of buildings were fortified for defence because they did not have to be because they were simply people's houses. Does that clear it up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, I think I see it clearly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have no questions to ask you. We would like to thank you for your testimony and send you back to your responsibilities. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now ask the usher to accompany the witness out of the courtroom and once he has left, we can adjourn our hearing. I now turn again to the Prosecutor. I think the pause comes at a good time because arrangements have to be taken for the maximum protection of the next witness for whom protective measures were asked. Is that not correct, Mr. Cayley, for the following witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a question I would like to ask you, because some time back when you raised your objection, you pointed to the indictment. I would like to point out to you that in the French version, I do not have the modified copy of the indictment since the last changes that were made, perhaps there were some translations problems, is that why?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we took advantage of the fact that there were no hearings in the Blaskic case in order to make available to the Trial Chamber an integrated version with the corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, we can now take a break until 4.35 p.m. (4.25 p.m.) (A short break) (4.35 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is Mr. Kehoe who is going to ask the questions? Am I right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will ask the usher to have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just take one moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a bit of a technical problem with the equipment. There was a minor accident at the break. It appears that the microphone -- the equipment is not working here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have the impression that when there are protective measures, that this involves everybody, but we have had a month to get the technical aspects into -- at a level where they are not going to give us problems any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately your Honour, there is no accounting for a pitcher of water. That will gum up the works every time. I think we are all set at this point, judge. We will recall witness D. I do believe we have to drop the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we have the witness brought in and, exceptionally, this time we are going to have the witness sit down immediately. But the witness will not come in until the curtains have been drawn. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness D, good afternoon. You are under the protection of the International Tribunal at the request of the Prosecution that has asked you to come, and has asked for special protective measures which were justified and granted. You will now start answering the questions. It is a public hearing, we can raise the curtains, but you are completely protected, and answer the questions that the Prosecutor is going to ask you, the Prosecutor, who asked you to come to testify in the trial against General Blaskic. Mr. Kehoe, as I recall, witness D, you have already taken the oath, therefore you are under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask for the microphone to the put on, please. The microphone is on? Yes. Mr. Kehoe, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe there are facial as well as oral distortions, just for the record. (redacted) when we had you here the last time, as the President just noted, you had been placed under oath and I believe you

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: getting a job, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. (Pause). (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992, after that, did you join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you joined the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you joined the Territorial Defence, did you serve on occasion at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What line did you serve in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We do not hear the answer because the microphone was not on. Do you hear me, witness D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said you served on the front-line, what was the front-line you served on? What front-line did you serve on first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I was in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we held the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After Visoko, did you serve on any other front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Turbe on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When were you on the front-line in Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the new year, 1992/1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were HVO soldiers also on the front-line at Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were at lines that were behind our backs, four or five kilometres approximately behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you were at the line in Turbe and you left the line in Turbe, did you come back to the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I came back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this at the time that conflict was taking place in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Between January of 1993 and April 1993, did you go back to any front-line again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear me? Does the French booth hear me? Yes, go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that between January 1993 and April 1993, you never went to the front-line again, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the hostilities broke out on the morning of 16th April 1993, were you still in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you on active duty on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you on leave at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take us directly to 16th April 1993. Can you tell the judges exactly what happened, beginning in the morning of 16th April 1993? Can you wait one moment. (Pause). Go ahead

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 16th April, I was at home, I was asleep (redacted) (redacted) shooting about 5.30 in the morning woke me up. There was shooting all over the place. One could hear detonations, rifle fire, I woke up (redacted), I got up, (redacted). From the window I looked in the direction where we heard the shooting and I saw smoke coming from (redacted) and one could hear terrible shooting. I told (redacted) (redacted), so that we could go into the basement because we had a kind of shelter that we made, because we were afraid of Serb aggression. I went into the yard of my house, (redacted) (redacted (redacted), and our other neighbours were there as well, women and children were still in the houses, but the men gathered there and we were discussing how to get organised and what to do in order to protect our families and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. Were you and all the people that were gathered to talk about what you were doing, were you all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So from where you were in (redacted), you could hear the firing and the smoke coming from the village of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you and your neighbours and family met to gather and discuss what to do, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was shooting all over the place and bullets were flying around us too, because it was all over (redacted), from all directions. We agreed -- is something wrong with my tone? Something is wrong with my tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think your tone is fine. I do not have any problem with your tone. Mr. President, your Honours? I think it is a minor feedback on the headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lot of shooting around us, bullets were flying around us and we agreed that our families should be put into the basements of our houses until we saw what would happen next. My family went down into the basement (redacted) and these other people who were staying (redacted), refugees and others, they all went to the basement. (redacted) were outside. We were simply waiting to see what would happen. We all went into the yard of a relative of mine, and at that point in time, it was perhaps about 7.00 or already 7.30, we heard somebody banging at the door of our neighbour who lived across the street and we heard his name being called out. He was there with us. His family was in his house where they were banging at the door. He went towards them, he put his hands in the air. He crossed the street and he went towards his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One moment, (Pause). Continue on, You said he crossed the street and he went toward his home; what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was looking in his direction and I saw four or five people walking up to him, they were wearing camouflage uniforms and some of them wore black uniforms, too, uniforms that were totally black. They had socks over -- stockings over their heads, their faces, so I could not recognise them. I went to the basement of the house of this relative of mine and soon after that, perhaps after a minute or two, we heard terrible firing and also an explosion, and then there was a kind of cease-fire. After that, there was a lot of shooting again from the direction of Kolonija, the residential area of the town of Vitez, and this went on for about ten minutes or so, this shooting, and I went from (redacted) (redacted) house so that I could be with (redacted) and with my parents. At that point, when I came into the house, very soon after that, then the family of this neighbour of mine who had crossed the street came,(redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). All of them came running, worried, bewildered, with bare feet, without any shoes. They were crying and we asked them what had happened and they told us that this neighbour of mine went into his home, took a rifle and started shooting at these soldiers from the balcony of his house and that they ran away, and that the soldiers fired back. As we were talking to them, the neighbourhood shot at them came too. Soon afterwards came (redacted). When we looked in that direction, the direction of their houses, we saw they were already on fire. During this shooting with these bullets, the houses caught fire and they burned down very quickly. We were all afraid, we were all terrified, and we were talking to this neighbour of ours and we suggested to him that he should go elsewhere, that he should hide somewhere else, so that if the HVO army came, they would not find him with us because he was the one who shot at them and he agreed to that and he went away from our houses in the direction of Kolonija, towards town. During that day, we were expecting the army, soldiers to come to our houses any minute. However, nobody came. We spent the night there in these houses. We all slept in the basements. Hardly anybody got much sleep really, because we were all afraid of the night and we did not know what would happen during the night and what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say you expected soldiers to come, did you say HVO soldiers or Armija soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I meant HVO soldiers. However, nobody came during the night, so we spent the night there and the next day, throughout the morning of the next day, nobody came. We heard shooting from all over, but we did not move anywhere, we all stayed in the yards of these houses so we did not know what was happening. We were simply sealed off, in a way. We could not move anywhere. This next day, in the afternoon, we were in the basements of these houses when we heard somebody banging at the door of the shop that was in (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is the next day, 17th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard somebody banging at the door of that part (redacted), so (redacted) got out of the basement and he went upstairs to see what was there, what was going on. He came back very soon to the basement, he was accompanied by a soldier and he said everybody should get out of the basement of (redacted) house and that everybody should move to my house, which is a bit lower, (redacted) (redacted). The soldier said that they would not torch my house but that they would torch (redacted), and that was why we were all supposed to move to my house. Everybody left except for me and a neighbour man, who was a younger man, because we were simply afraid to leave, we were afraid of being captured or killed or whatever. We stayed in the house until water started dripping into the basement, probably the pipelines broke down and we also felt smoke in the basement, so we could not stay there any longer, so we decided to move on to my house. This neighbour of mine and I ran in the direction of my house, and when I saw that in my house, (redacted) were not there, I asked where they were. (redacted) me that they went to my relative's house, which was safer, it had a better basement, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (redacted) let me stop you for a second. You just testified that the HVO soldier came and said that the house that you were in, in the basement, was going to be burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But that your house was not going to be burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for that, why your house would not be burnt and your father's house would be burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house is made -- was made in such a way that it faced two directions, and Muslims usually say that houses should face four directions and they would leave those houses facing only two directions and they would not burn them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So (redacted) had a four-sided roof and (redacted) had a two-sided roof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the HVO soldier said he was going to burn down your (redacted) house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the burning down of (redacted) house, had any HVO soldiers come to take your vehicles, automobiles from the premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before this soldier came who told us we should get out of the basement, a group of soldiers came and they were also banging at the door and (redacted) went out and they asked for the car keys, because (redacted) had a car in my garage and (redacted) had a car in the garage. I told (redacted) where the keys were, and (redacted) where the keys were. However, he was probably too afraid, he did not manage to find the keys and we heard him being hit. (redacted) followed him and went into my house, took the keys for both cars and handed the keys over to them, they took the car from my garage and this car that was in (redacted) garage is one that I had broken down on purpose, because HVO soldiers would take cars from Muslims who had good cars, so I had broken it down so they could not take it. They came, they tried to turn it on, but they did not manage to ignite it, so one of them fired at the car and then they left. Then this single soldier came and said that (redacted) (redacted) house should be torched and that we should all go to my house that they would not burn. When I came to my house, I realised that (redacted) were not there and I asked (redacted) where they were. They told me that they went to my relative's house. I decided to go to my relative's house too. It is about 150 metres away from my house. I ran across the garden and I came to my relative's house, I went into the basement. I spent two or three minutes there, perhaps, when my relative who stood at the door to the basement said that HVO soldiers were in my yard and that they were taking all the men out of my house and that they were lining them up by the fence. I peeked through the door a bit and I saw (redacted), my neighbour and these refugees who were staying (redacted), I saw them being lined up along the fence of my yard. I went to my relative's basement once again and we sat there waiting for them to come and get us too. However, no one came to get us. They had already torched that house as well, they did not even warn us, they did not even tell us about it, that my relative's house was on fire. Again, water started dripping and we felt the smoke again, so we had to leave the basement of that house and we went out. It was already getting dark, and my relative's house was already burning, (redacted) house and my neighbours' houses were burning. Four houses were burning at the same time, and we went into the yard of this house and we heard tanks coming down the road. We ran out into the road and we saw them coming from Rijeka, three tanks coming from the direction of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there before you go into telling us about the tanks. All the houses that were on fire, were they Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were all the men that were being taken prisoner, were they all Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened when you saw the tanks coming down the road from Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Rijeka, there were tanks coming and I took (redacted) in my hands, in my arms, I stood in front of the tanks and they all stopped and we all expected them to protect us, to save us, but they started moving backwards. With my left hand, I held on to the gun of the tank, because these were small calibre guns. The tank was dragging me along for about 150 metres. I ran after it so I could not take it much longer and I just let it go. Then the tank stopped, turned around and then they went back in the direction of Rijeka. I came back to this group of women and children, the houses were burning, we could not even stand in the middle of the road any more, the flames were so strong and we decided to take shelter in the house of a neighbour of ours, a Croat. We went into his yard and we asked him whether we could stay with him and he said yes. So then we took shelter there in his house, we spent about 15 or 20 minutes there, when another neighbour of ours came and said we should all move to his house and that we would be safe in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many people moved to this other neighbour's house? How many Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 50 or 60 of us altogether, including the women and children from all the Muslim houses there, we were all together in one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go to this second neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we all went there and we stayed there and around 12.00 at night until 2.00, I was staying in a room upstairs. It was a very big house. And I decided to go downstairs, where my neighbour was and as I was walking down the stairs, the main door to the house opened and there was a HVO soldier there. He asked me how come I was there. I said that I was staying there now with this neighbour, and he said that I was supposed to come with him, and that another boy, a young man of 17 who was a refugee, should also come with me. I went upstairs, I called this young man and I told (redacted) that I had to come along with this soldier and that I did not know where I was going. We all went downstairs and we started moving towards the main road. When we came on to the main road, the soldier told us that we should put our hands up above our heads, and that we should walk along the middle of the road. We started moving in the direction of Rijeka of Sumarija. As we were approaching the veterinary station, Sumarija, the soldier told us to stop. We stopped and he told me that I and this boy should go to his house. Because I did not know exactly which house was his, I said I did not know which house was his and then this young man who was with me said that he knew which house was his and he said we should go to his house and that he would go to Sumarija and that there was a HVO patrol down there. So we went to his house, I knocked at the door and the mother of this soldier opened the door and I said that he had sent us there and she said "no problem whatsoever, please come in". When I walked into the house, I found that neighbour of mine who was together with me in the basement of my house and who was captured by HVO soldiers before, I found him there too and very soon, two relatives of mine came in as well. We spent the night there; however, the next day the mother of this soldier who sent us to his house, this housewife, told us through tears, she was crying, that we had to leave their house, that on the radio they were told that no Croats were allowed to keep Muslims in their houses, and I said, "no problem, we will leave", but that somebody should take us to hand us over there. Soon the husband of this woman came and that is what she told him too and he said that that was out of the question, that he would not hand us over, but that we would stay at his house and he left. However, the woman was crying all the time and I decided not to stay there any longer, but as soon as her husband would come in, that he should hand me over. As soon as he came in, I told her I could not stay there any more, that I could not stay there any more and that he should take me to the veterinary station and hand me over there where all the other Muslims were. So he took me and my relative who was younger and my other relative who was older stayed on. My neighbour also stayed on, who was married to a (redacted). He brought us to the veterinary station and I was put in the basement of the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back to this radio broadcast, did the mother of this soldier tell you what the radio broadcast said about Croats hiding Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she told us that the radio was saying that no Croats were to harbour any Muslims and she was just afraid for her own safety and for the safety of her family and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about -- you went to the veterinary station. Tell us about the veterinary station and the conditions in the veterinary station when you got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was put in the basement of the veterinary station and all my friends and relatives, neighbours were there. My (redacted) was also there. Down in the basement, it was very tight, we could only crouch, we could not move around, we could only sit down and nothing else. It was damp down there, the air was stale. There was no ventilation, it was wet. Since we were too many, they said that the older people could move upstairs to the room where the animals were brought, and so (redacted) and other people went up there and it was better up there, the air was fresher. I stayed down in the basement, and I spent the night there, that night. But when I arrived there, I saw that some people from the neighbourhood were missing, ones that should have been there and I asked where they were and I was told that a group was taken to Santici to dig trenches. I spent the night there at the station and in the morning, a van arrived and a HVO soldier arrived and said that a group of people was needed to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the veterinary station, all the people you saw in the basement, were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all civilians. Nobody wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The people you said were taken -- they told you that people were taken out to dig trenches. What was the area they were taken to dig trenches at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took them to Ciganluk. This was in the direction of the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said the next day a minibus came to pick you and others up to dig trenches, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about 20 of us were assigned to dig trenches and we sat into this minibus and they took us down in the direction of the railway station. When we passed the railway station, we headed towards the village of Santici between Buhine Kuce and Santici. The minibus stopped in front of a house and a group of ten people got off and I stayed in the minibus and we were taken to the village of Santici. We were put in front of the house and we stayed there for about half an hour. They gave us some pickaxes and shovels and a soldier came and took us in the direction of Pirici. When we arrived to the village of Pirici, there was a house there where they had some sort of command, and there was an intersection in front of it of roads there in Pirici, so that was a larger open area, so we waited there for about ten minutes and this soldier came back and took us above this house towards the Muslim cemetery, and he assigned us to trench digging, and I was assigned with a friend to dig to the (redacted) side of the Muslim cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you first got up there, did you see any telephone lines or any means of communication between the HVO soldiers up in Pirici and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right there at the entrance of the Muslim cemetery was a telephone, and this is where we were waiting to be assigned and I was surprised, I asked the soldier whom I knew, "you have a telephone here", he said "yes, we do". He told me that just before that, he spoke with his wife who lived in the city of Vitez, so from this phone, they could call into Vitez, to the city, so the lines were connected through the main post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were then taken to dig trenches, is that right? If so, tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, myself and another friend were taken to (redacted) (redacted) and already the trenches had been started, somebody had started digging them before us, so we worked there until about noon. We widened the trenches and things like that and according to them, we were finished there, so then they returned us to the (redacted) and then they took us to (redacted) (redacted). We also dug trenches there. They also brought us some food there, there was some bread, so we ate. We were finished there quite quickly and then they took us in the direction of this command of theirs from where we had come and there we waited again for a while and then the whole group was taken in the direction from this command in Pirici, down towards the bungalows at the same level where that command of theirs was. My friend and I dug in a ravine, it was sheltered, so we were protected there and we could work there without any problem. When we were done, the HVO soldier that we had to go out into an open field and there was no protection there. We could be seen from all sides there. Myself and my friend went out there and started digging, I had a pickaxe, he had a shovel and I dug a bit and then he started shovelling it out. I was looking in the direction of a forest that was in front of us. It still did not have any foliage.
